● The hugo driver in ../ponder now finds Infusion through moduleOverrides.json5
  instead of the hard-coded ../fluid-infusion-6. The full build runs cleanly
  against your ../infusion-6 checkout (67 pages, about 3 seconds), in both
  static and --live true modes, and eslint infusion/js passes. Builds went to
  the scratchpad; I haven't regenerated docs-infusion.

  Changes in ponder (uncommitted):
  - infusion/site.html: the eight hand-listed Infusion <script> tags and the
    <fluid-module id="infusion-6"> are replaced by a single FluidBoot.js script,
    as fluid-view.md now describes. Its src points at
    ../node_modules/infusion-6/..., but that's only a placeholder: under node,
    the files are read from whichever checkout the build uses.
  - infusion/js/buildSite.js:
    - Infusion is now located in this order: --infusion <dir> if given, then the
      infusion-6 entry in the site's moduleOverrides.json5, then infusion-6
      installed in node_modules. This is the same order as Infusion's own
      bin/boot.js, plus the --infusion flag.
    - The overrides, plus Infusion itself, are passed as moduleSources to
      fluid.loadAndBootDocument, so each module's files come from its hot
      checkout.
    - The overrides file is parsed the same lightweight way FluidBoot.js does
      it, because Infusion's JSON5 reader can't be reached before Infusion has
      been found.
  - --limit / --from fix: these crashed in feeds.js, because the feeds were
    built from the truncated page list. They now use the full model.
  - infusion/README.md: the build instructions now describe how Infusion is
    located.

  What the comparison with the committed docs-infusion shows:
  - Missing fl-id-* ids: the new pages no longer carry these ids. That's a
    deliberate Infusion change from FLUID-7030
    (https://github.com/fluid-project/infusion-6/issues/30), so the committed
    copy is just stale.
  - Attribute order: inside the markdown content, attributes come out in a
    different order. This has no effect on how the pages display.

  Run npm run build-infusion to refresh docs-infusion when you're ready.

  Without a moduleOverrides.json5 or --infusion, the build needs infusion-6
  installed in node_modules. It isn't in ponder's package.json dependencies yet,
  so that fallback currently stops with a module-not-found error.

❯ OK, it is time for the BIG ONE. Read https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research 
  /wp-content/uploads/2018/03/build-systems.pdf and also the commentary files   
       a-scratch/reports/reconciling-build-systems.md                           
          a-scratch/reports/static-site-live-preview.md                         
          a-scratch/reports/visual-layout-static-site.md . Our goal is to       
  bridge the gap between the static site generation currently performed in the  
  ponder-infusion branch, and fully live visual editing, backed by optimistic   
  concurrency and isomorphic rendering. The essential bridge is that we will    
  produce a Chrome extension, "Edit in Infusion" which when activated on a      
  suitable statically rendered site such as this one, will inject code into the 
  document broadcasting a $linkage record, which through adding a mixin layer   
  named such as fluid.withEditing, will cause the page to migrate in place to   
  an editable version of itself. Content blocks of different kinds, e.g. those  
  backed by markdown, will upgrade to rich text editors which still nonetheless 
  bidirectionally synchronise to markdown. You can see primitive versions of    
  this backed by CodeMirror 5 in the demo/compose-edit demo. There will also be 
  a visual block-oriented affordance to add new blocks into the document much   
  in the style of divi builder or TinaCMS. Where there are "collections" in the 
  site, such as blog posts, there will be a UI to allocate a new one together   
  with choosing its name, with a "shadow URL" system that anticipates the       
  static URL that will in the end result, but which patches it with a # variant 
  addressing the as yet unpublished file name. Similar to our current curation  
  workflow in saanich-peninsula-flora/src/curation there will be an optimistic  
  concurrency system that makes it appear that any edits have been              
  instantaneously made by storing them in IndexedDB, whilst the GitHub Action   
  republishing the site churns away. They will remain previewable but with a    
  distinct styling indicating that they are either uncommitted edits, or        
  committed edits which have not yet been published, until the Action           
  completes. Survey the reactive build system taxonomy in the paper to scope    
  out what variety of reactive/build system (trace forming, etc.) we need to    
  upgrade to in order to lay our current purely in-memory reactivity alongside  
  a proper externalised build system that is capable of tracking which pieces   
  of work have been accomplished with what data dependencies, so that the       
  isomorphic build system currently operated by Infusion's hydrate.js can       
  properly advertise and cooperate with its avatar on the client. Right now we  
  want a kind of "minimum viable product" with some working component at each   
  of the architectural points - the GitHub Action + CloudFlare worker (consult  
  imerss-cloudflare for this), the Chrome extension, and the actual process of  
  injection, the client laying its hands on the raw layer structure of the      
  page, advertising the linkage, having the UI adapt, accept updates of a       
  simple kind, post them back, and see the different visual states as the       
  Action runs. Draw up a work list for this work, together with any further     
  research and experiments necessary, write it to                               
  a-scratch/reports/0-live-static-editing.md, and begin on it.

● I've written the work list to a-scratch/reports/0-live-static-editing.md and
  built a first pass at the MVP for the static-site side and the Chrome
  extension. The site side is tested; the extension has only passed syntax
  checks, because there's no Chromium on this machine to run it. Nothing is
  committed and nothing has been pushed to GitHub or deployed.

  Where we sit in the paper's taxonomy. Within one process, Infusion's cell
  graph is already Shake's cell in memory: a suspending scheduler, dependencies
  discovered as cells run, verifying traces, and early cutoff when a value comes
  out unchanged. It is also better self-tracking than Shake, because layers are
  data. But nothing survives between builds: each run of buildSite.js rebuilds
  every page from scratch, like the paper's busy. Its only saving is not
  rewriting files whose output is unchanged, which is Make's trick.

  The plan therefore moves in two steps:
  1. Persistent verifying traces, published with the site. For each page, record
     the hashes of the inputs it was built from, and publish that beside the
     site.
  2. Suspending scheduler with constructive traces. This is the paper's empty
     "Cloud Shake" cell. The published site acts as the shared cache, and the
     client is a second builder running the same tasks. Deep constructive traces
     are ruled out, because they lose early cutoff and allow the paper's
     "Frankenbuild".

  A useful result falls out of step 1: an edit counts as published when the
  deployed trace records the hash of the edited text. That replaces the
  claimStatus.json list used in curation.

  What exists now:
  - ponder:
    - infusion/js/trace.js writes docs/fluid-trace.json and puts a linkage
      record (repo, branch, source path and hash, editable blocks) into the head
      of every page that has a source file.
    - siteModel.js gives each page its source path and computes source hashes.
    - Post content containers are marked data-fluid-block="markdown".
    - infusion/linkage.json names the repo and branch to edit.
    - .github/workflows/build-site.yml rebuilds the site and commits docs/
      whenever sources change.
    - Tested: a full build writes 67 pages, the trace and the linkage records,
      and the hashes match the content files.
  - infusion-6 extension/edit-in-infusion/ (Manifest V3):
    - The content script finds the linkage record, shows any saved edit over the
      published block (dashed amber for uncommitted, pulsing blue for
      committed, red for conflict), and opens an editor panel with live markdown
      preview.
    - Commits go through the GitHub Contents API with the expected blob sha;
      GitHub refuses with a 409 if the file has changed, which gives the
      optimistic concurrency.
    - It polls the trace until it records the edit, then drops the edit and
      reloads the page.
    - Saved edits and the GitHub token live in the service worker, not the
      content script. A content script's IndexedDB belongs to the page's origin,
      so the page could otherwise read or tamper with them.
    - A README.md explains how to load it unpacked.

  Before it runs end to end:
  - Browser test: the end-to-end script is written and waiting in the
    scratchpad. It covers activate, edit, reload, a simulated commit, and the
    trace catching up. Running it needs puppeteer's Chromium (about 150 MB into
    ~/.cache/puppeteer, outside the project), which your own test:browser-qunit
    also lacks. Shall I download it?
  - package-lock.json: the Action runs npm ci, so the lock file has to be
    regenerated with npm install now that infusion-6 is a dependency.
  - Your setup: a fine-grained GitHub token, entered in the extension's options.
    Sign-in through the existing Cloudflare worker comes later, and needs the
    extension's origin added to its allowed origins in curation.tf, then tofu 
    apply.
  - Branch: linkage records point edits at ponder-infusion, but Pages presumably
    publishes from main. Until the branch is merged, testing means serving
    docs/ locally.

  Known gaps in this pass:
  - The extension's preview uses its own copy of markdown-it, without the
    build's heading ids or fence-option stripping, and shortcodes render as
    empty blocks. The fix is item 12: one markdown pipeline shared by the build
    and the client.
  - Pages migrating in place via fluid.withEditing (item 13) is not started yet.
    This pass edits the DOM directly as a stand-in.
  - fluid-trace.json lists each page's inputs coarsely; deriving them from the
    cell graph instead is research item R1.

  extracted text, and the scratchpad also holds a 76-line PDF-scraping script

● Yes, there is. Its browser was already downloaded, into
  node_modules/.cache/puppeteer as set in infusion-6's .puppeteerrc.cjs.
  Puppeteer finds that config by searching from the directory it runs in. I'd
  run the test from the scratchpad, so it looked in the default
  ~/.cache/puppeteer and found nothing. Nothing needs downloading; I was wrong
  to suggest it.

  Run from the infusion-6 checkout, the end-to-end test of the extension passed
  every step. It ran against the build served locally:

  1. The page's linkage record is found, and its hash matches the content file.
  2. Activating the editor reads the source from GitHub (one public read, no
     token).
  3. An edit re-renders the post's content live and is held as an uncommitted
     edit (dashed amber outline). It is still shown after a reload.
  4. Committing without a token reports that a token is missing, and the edit
     stays uncommitted.
  5. I simulated a commit inside the extension. The page then showed it as
     committed (pulsing blue).
  6. I rewrote the local fluid-trace.json to record the edit's hash. Within one
     15-second poll the page showed "Published", reloaded, and no saved edits
     remained.

  The committed label also showed the earlier "No GitHub token" message. That
  came from my simulated commit copying the old message; a real commit clears
  it.

  Still untested: a real commit, and the 409 refusal GitHub gives when the file
  has changed underneath an edit. Both write to GitHub, so they need your token
  and a test branch you choose. I've updated the progress note in
  0-live-static-editing.md to match.

  code, and in headless Chromium all 49 of ponder's content files render
  identically under node and in the browser.

  - One pipeline: the markdown setup that lived inside siteModel.js is now
    infusion/js/markdown.js, a single file that works under node and in the
    browser. The build uses it and its output is byte-identical to before. I
    removed the old siteModel.headingId and expandShortcodes; nothing else
    called them.
  - Published with the site: the build copies the pipeline, with the same
    versions of markdown-it and its plugins, into docs/js/fluid-markdown/. Each
    page's linkage record names those scripts, and because markdown.js is part
    of the site's templates, changing it changes the trace's template hash.
  - The extension uses it: the extension no longer bundles its own markdown-it.
    A small bridge script (js/bridge.js) loads the site's scripts into the page
    and renders with them. That fixes the missing heading ids: the edited post's
    preview now has its 21.

  Problem found on the way: under Manifest V3, a script element a content script
  inserts must obey the extension's security policy, which admits only the
  extension's own files. So the browser refused the site's markdown scripts at
  first. The bridge can be inserted because it's an extension file, and scripts
  the bridge inserts obey the page's own policy instead. I've added this to
  research item R6 in the plan.

  Shortcode figures: the pipeline renders them as empty placeholders. The
  preview now swaps in the published figure whenever its shortcode parameters
  are unchanged, which is safe because a figure's rendering depends only on
  those parameters.

  The extension's end-to-end test passes on a post with four figures, all four
  now shown in the preview.

  Two differences remain between a preview and the built page:
  - URLs: links and image paths aren't made relative, because the build does
    that as a separate pass after rendering.
  - Code blocks: they aren't syntax-highlighted, because highlight.js only runs
    when the page first loads.

  Both should go away with item 13, booting Infusion over the page so it renders
  the block itself; that would also replace the figure-swapping. Old copies of
  the published pipeline scripts also aren't cleaned out of docs/ yet.

  Still untested is a real commit and the 409 conflict GitHub returns when the
  file has changed underneath an edit. Both need your token and a branch you
  choose. The plan's progress section in 0-live-static-editing.md is updated.

      829    relative URL of the site's root in its `fluid-site-root` att
           ribute, e.g. `"../../"`, so that in the browser the page
      830    recognises its own location wherever the site is served from
           , even from local files.
      831 
      832 +**Site-absolute URLs.** In a page recording its site's root, e
          +very `href` and `src` which rendering writes and which        
      833 +begins with a single `/`, e.g. `/css/main.css`, is resolved ag
          +ainst that root as it is written, e.g. to                     
      834 +`../../css/main.css`. This applies alike to URLs bound in temp
          +lates, to those in verbatim markup such as content            
      835 +rendered from markdown, and to those islands render. Templates
          + and content can therefore name the site's resources          
      836 +site-absolutely, and the page still works wherever the site is
          + served from, with no pass over the output, as Hugo's         
      837 +`relativeURLs` makes. The browser resolves them against the sa
          +me attribute, so a page made live renders the same URLs as    
      838 +the build wrote. Protocol-relative URLs (`//host/...`), absolu
          +te URLs and relative URLs are left as written, as is          
      839 +everything in a page which records no site root.              
      840 +                                                              
      841  Under node, the view creates a fresh **output document** while
            `documentLocation` is available, and releases it when
      842  the location becomes unavailable or the view is destroyed. A c
           hanged location creates a fresh document. Every output
      843  document is listed in the cell `fluid.outputDocuments`, as rec
           ords `{dokkument, location, url}`, in order of creation.

● Done. A final look at what changed in each working tree:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● I made both changes you asked for: the build now gets relative URLs right as
  it renders, and editing a post now migrates its content block in place into a
  live Infusion component. On a post with figures, the migrated block is
  byte-identical to what the build wrote. Nothing is committed.

  Relative URLs: yes, the build gets them right first time now. Infusion makes
  every href or src that starts with a single / relative to the page's site root
  as it writes it. That covers templates, markdown content and shortcode
  islands alike, under node and in the browser. ponder's URL post-pass is gone
  and the output is byte-identical to what it produced. Static builds now keep
  the small fluid-site-root attribute this relies on. There's a new view test,
  and I documented the behaviour in content/docs/fluid-view.md.

  Migration in place (item 13):
  - Build: the site publishes Infusion's browser files and its own SFCs under
    content-hashed directories in docs/js/. Each page's linkage record names
    them, and each editable block names its component's layers (ponder.content).
  - Extension: it boots that Infusion inside the page, then creates
    fluid.editRoot, whose $linkage adds fluid.withEditing to every
    ponder.content component, as you described. Each block's component is then
    booted over the block from its markdown source. From then on Infusion
    renders edits; the extension no longer writes the block itself.
  - Cost: nothing loads until there is something to show: a saved edit, or a
    source fetched on opening the editor whose hash matches the page.

  Two Infusion bugs found and fixed along the way, both in FluidView.js:
  - Duplicate figure components: Infusion's page-wide self-boot created a second
    component over each figure while the figure's SFC was still loading. That
    component had no shortcode parameters, so it blanked the figure's src, alt,
    link and caption. Self-boot now skips island elements. I only reproduced
    this race in the browser; no unit test catches it.
  - Lost figure style: while the figure's template loaded, the surrounding
    content stripped the style the figure had written into the built markup. The
    new test fails without this fix.

  Tests: I ran the full edit cycle (edit, reload, commit state, publication) in
  headless Chromium on three posts, and all pass:

  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         Post         │                 After migration                  │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Two figures          │ Block byte-identical to the build's output       │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Stabilization widget │ Only difference: the widget's script gains the   │
  │                      │ fluid-client marker that static builds strip     │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ships its own copy   │ Not migrated, by design; edits are previewed as  │
  │ of Infusion          │ before, figures included                         │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  npm test gives 2416/2419. The 3 failures are tldraw "Ask me anything" tests
  that fail the same way on the committed code. The view tests pass 59/59 in
  Chromium.

  Not solved yet (recorded in the plan as new research items):
  - R9, page-script output: migration takes ownership of the block, so it
    removes anything the page's own scripts added after load. That means the
    heading anchors ponder.js adds, and the panels the stabilization widget
    builds, which disappear. Infusion needs a way to mark DOM as owned by client
    code.
  - R8, pages with their own Infusion: the reactivity post loads an older
    vendored copy of Infusion for its demos. A second copy can't be loaded, so
    that page is edited without migration.
  - Late boot: Infusion started booting before its SFC parser had loaded, cached
    the failure and never recovered. The extension works around it by declaring
    the SFCs only after every file has loaded; Infusion could defer its boot
    instead.
  - Stale published files: old hashed copies of the published files (about 2 MB
    per build) aren't pruned from docs/js/ yet.

  One thing to check: ponder's working tree shows changes to many files in docs/
  and to package-lock.json that I didn't make. All my builds wrote to the
  scratchpad, and there's no docs/fluid-trace.json, so they don't come from the
  new build. I've left them alone. Did you run a build or npm install in the
  meantime?

● That patch is removed now; FluidView.js is back to its earlier state for this
  work.

  What fluid-client is. It's an attribute Infusion already uses, mainly on
  <script> elements: it marks a script as payload for the browser alone. Under
  node, Infusion writes such a script into the page but never runs it, and
  fluid.classifyScriptNode reports it as a "client" script. ponder uses it for
  KaTeX, giscus, and the stabilization shortcode's stabilization-regimes.js. The
  static build strips the marker, as the one difference after migration showed.

  The patch I'd started tried to widen it to mean "this DOM belongs to client
  code": an element marked fluid-client would keep its children, and nodes the
  page's scripts add (heading anchors) would survive Infusion claiming the
  markup. That's the renderer special-casing you want to avoid, and your
  suggestion removes the need.

  Your suggestion. Converting the inline examples into self-booting components
  does remove the need, for both cases where migration currently wipes
  something:
  - The reactivity demo: it would become an island component (a shortcode SFC,
    like the figure). Its template renders the target element and an effect
    boots the visualiser into it. Migrating the page then creates a fresh
    instance whose effect boots the demo again, rather than the content
    reconciling away DOM it doesn't know about. The cost is that the demo
    restarts from scratch when you start editing.
  - The stabilization widget: the same treatment. Its fluid-client script's
    setup becomes the component's effect.
  - Heading anchors: these aren't an inline example but ponder.js adding them
    after load. The cleanest fix is for the shared markdown pipeline to render
    them, so they're part of the built markup and of every migrated rendering,
    and ponder.js stops adding them.

  One consequence. A self-booting component only runs if the page boots
  Infusion, so these pages would load Infusion through FluidBoot.js. At the
  moment they only load FluidCore and FluidSignals for the demo. The extension
  would then find that Infusion already booted and use it rather than load any
  of it. That's simpler than the bridge change I made earlier this turn, which
  skips framework files the page already loaded. I'd revert it in favour of "if
  the site's Infusion is already booted, use it", and treat any other Infusion
  as unsupported, in line with what you said about versions.

  Two things from earlier in this turn are still in place:
  - The reactivity post now loads current Infusion files from one copy the build
    publishes at docs/js/infusion-6/, rather than the vendored
    static/infusion-6/, which I deleted. In Chromium it behaves identically to
    infusion-6's own gallery page, with no errors.
  - docs/ has been rebuilt with that change.

  Shall I go ahead with the conversion: the reactivity demo and stabilization
  widget as self-booting components, anchors from the pipeline, and the bridge
  reusing an already-booted Infusion?

● The reactivity post now runs on current Infusion, and every page now survives
  migration in place without losing anything its scripts used to add. The two
  live widgets became self-booting components, and the heading anchors and code
  highlighting moved into the build. I rebuilt docs/. Nothing is committed.

  One Infusion per site. The build now publishes a single copy of the Infusion
  that built the site, at docs/js/infusion-6/, laid out like the checkout. It
  includes exactly the files content or SFCs refer to, and a reference to a
  missing file fails the build. The vendored static/infusion-6/ is deleted, and
  so is FluidDebugging.js. Migration stands down on any page holding a different
  Infusion, rather than trying to support it.

  Live widgets are now components. Each boots its widget from a $bindable once
  rendered. Its libraries are browser-only scripts of its SFC, so the build
  never evaluates them.
  - Reactivity visualiser: a new {{< vizreactive >}} shortcode, loading
    infusion-6's visualiser as its own gallery page does.
  - Stabilization widget: stabilization-regimes.js moved beside its SFC and now
    exports boot(stage).
  - Which pages load Infusion: only a page holding one of these islands boots
    it, importing only the SFCs it needs. Other pages load no Infusion, and the
    extension reuses a page's Infusion rather than loading it again.

  Built in rather than added by page scripts:
  - Heading anchors: the markdown pipeline renders them, and static/js/ponder.js
    is deleted. Headings in templates (post titles in lists, "see also") lose
    their anchors; those pointed at # and did nothing.
  - Code highlighting: the pipeline runs highlight.js's own highlightBlock on
    each code block, under node and in the browser. All 147 code blocks on the
    24 pages with code are identical to what the browser used to produce on
    load.

  Two bugs found and fixed along the way:
  - Second free component: edit.js reset each block's HTML on start-up even when
    it had changed nothing, so the page booted a second component over each
    island.
  - Destroy not taking effect: destroying a component only takes effect when the
    graph next stabilises, and nothing prompted that. The bridge now does.

  Test results:
  - Without the extension: both widget posts run on current Infusion with no
    errors. The visualiser matches infusion-6's own page exactly, and the
    stabilization panels render.
  - With the extension, on four posts (plain, two figures, the stabilization
    widget, and the reactivity post with its visualiser and four figures):
    - The full cycle passes: migrate, edit, reload, commit state, publication.
    - Infusion is loaded once, no stray components remain, and both widgets
      re-boot after migration.
    - On the plain and figure posts the migrated block is identical to the
      build's output. On the widget posts it differs only inside the widget's
      own live DOM.
  - Pipeline: all 49 content files render identically under node and in the
    browser.
  - Infusion: npm test gives 2416/2419; the 3 failures are the tldraw tests that
    also fail on the committed code. The view tests pass 59/59 in Chromium.
  - Lint and links: lint is clean, and a local check found no broken internal
    links. I didn't run ponder's npm test, because checklinks.js fetches every
    external link.

  The build also now prunes old hashed directories and pipeline scripts from
  docs/js/.

  Still to know:
  - Hugo layouts: Hugo's own layouts still refer to the moved stabilization
    script, and Hugo has no vizreactive shortcode, so Hugo can no longer build
    these two posts. This branch's build is Infusion's, so I left them alone.
  - Widget state on edit: starting to edit a widget page restarts its widget.
    That's the price of the component approach.
  - Late boot: the race where Infusion starts booting before its SFC parser has
    loaded is still handled only by the extension's workaround.
  - Next items: a real commit against a test branch, booting whole pages so list
    pages can migrate, and forming traces from the cell graph. The plan in
    0-live-static-editing.md records all of this.

  Traces from the cell graph (R1):

    inputs, tested by a new npm run document-trace-test:
    - the model values it read, by path;
    - only the keys of a list that a $for iterates;
    - reads through valueAs aliases and through arguments, resolved to the model
      path they really read;
    - shared site-level computations, by their value;
    - the layers and templates it used.
  - In ponder's build: each build writes docs/fluid-build-trace.json and reports
    which documents' inputs changed. Pages are keyed by permalink, and SFC
    layers are hashed by their file's text. Repeat builds are deterministic.
  - Soundness check: I made temporary edits to one post, then restored it.
    - Body edit: exact, with 3 pages flagged and the same 3 rewritten.
    - Title edit: sound but imprecise, with 49 flagged for 5 rewritten. Every
      page reads the shared related-posts index (relatedIndex), which holds
      every title.
  - ponder changes to make this precise: a site-level relatedIndex, so pages no
    longer depend on every page whole. Summary text now has its HTML entities
    decoded, a bug the client boot exposed.
  - Infusion fixes: two found along the way, recording values as plain data and
    hashing them stably.

  Whole-page boot (R2), in progress:
  - Built: every page now has a linkage record and a model slice (*.model.json):
    its config, its own record, the pages it read, and the shared values it
    read.
  - Experiment: in Chromium, booting ponder.site from the slice re-renders a
    single post identically to the static page.
  - Still differing:
    - Home page: the content puts an <h2> inside <a> inside <p>. The browser's
      parser restructures that when loading the static page; Infusion's template
      parser keeps it as written.
    - /post/ list: a summary holds <programming 2026>, which the two parsers
      likewise treat differently.
    - 404 page: an inline script fills the emoji after load, and the boot clears
      it.
    - Sibling documents: a vizreactive island stays pending in another document
      booted alongside list pages.
  - Not wired in: the extension doesn't use whole-page boot yet.

  Also left:
  - Title-edit precision: needs early cutoff at the per-page related-posts
    computation.
  - Skipping unchanged pages: an incremental build that doesn't render them
    still needs booting each document on its own.
  - A real commit: still untested against a test branch.

  The plan's progress section records this state. My experiment scripts are in
  the scratchpad's tools/ folder.

● Both are unchanged by this round, and neither has been fixed in Infusion.

  Widget state on edit

  What happens. On a page with a live widget (the reactivity visualiser, the
  stabilization animation), the page boots Infusion itself. Each widget island
  becomes a free component, and its $bindable starts the widget in that island.

  When you start editing, the block's content component takes over the block and
  allocates its islands as its own children. To avoid two components on one
  element, the bridge first destroys the page's free island components. Their
  unbind stops each widget and clears its DOM, and the new island children then
  bind afresh.

  So the widget restarts from scratch: the visualiser loses whichever fixture
  and step you'd reached, and the animation starts again. The page looks the
  same, but the interaction state is lost.

  Status. Unchanged. The whole-page boot experiment does the same handover
  (destroy, then boot afresh), so it has the same effect. Nothing in this round
  addressed it.

  The likely fix. Hand the existing island component over rather than recreate
  it. When the block's component meets an island that a free component already
  renders, with the same layers and parameters, it could take that component as
  its child instead of allocating a fresh one. The bound widget would then
  survive untouched. This needs an Infusion mechanism to adopt an existing
  component at an island's place, and I haven't checked what Infusion already
  offers for injecting an existing component there. The alternative,
  transferring a $bindable's bound value between components, seems more fragile.

  Late boot

  What happens. FluidView-browser.js calls fluid.bootDocument as its last act.
  That defers to DOMContentLoaded, unless the page has already loaded, in which
  case it boots at once. In FluidBoot.js's list of files, FluidView-browser.js
  comes before template-parser.js and sfc-parser.js.

  - Normal page: FluidBoot.js writes all the script tags while the page is
    parsing, so every file has loaded before DOMContentLoaded, and the order
    doesn't matter.
  - Infusion loaded into an already-loaded page (what the extension does): boot
    runs the moment FluidView-browser.js arrives. If imports are declared by
    then, their SFCs are fetched straight away. Their parse can then run before
    fluid.parseHTMLToTree exists. The failure is stored as the parse effect's
    value, and nothing ever retries it, so the component sits at "Injection in
    progress" forever.

  Status. Still handled only by the extension's workaround. The bridge declares
  the modules and imports after every framework file has loaded, then calls
  fluid.acquireModules and fluid.docToImportMap itself; the whole-page boot
  experiment does the same. Two things changed around it this round, without
  fixing it:
  - Pages with live islands now boot Infusion the normal way, through
    FluidBoot.js at parse time, so they never hit it.
  - On such a page, the extension reuses the Infusion already there rather than
    loading it late, so it doesn't hit it either.

  Fix options, in order of simplicity:
  1. Reorder FluidBoot.js's file list so the parsers come before
     FluidView-browser.js. I'd first check whether either parser depends on
     FluidView-browser.js; nothing I saw suggests it does.
  2. Start the boot only once the last framework file has loaded, so a late load
     can't boot early.
  3. Make the SFC parse effect retry once the parser becomes available. This is
     the most robust, but also the most work.

  Option 1 would let the bridge drop its workaround. I can make that change and
  add a browser test that loads Infusion into an already-loaded page, if you'd
  like.

● How booting Infusion finds its landmarks

  Booting over static markup does reconcile against the DOM, but only once, and
  it reuses what's there rather than rebuilding it.

  When a component's view first renders into a container that already holds
  markup, Infusion still activates its template, building the vnode tree and
  binding effects as usual. Then fluid.assignChildNodes claims the existing
  child nodes by position, on the expectation that the markup was rendered from
  the same template. A claimed node that matches its vnode's tag is reused as it
  is, and an attribute is written only if its value differs. Nothing is created
  or replaced unless it disagrees.

  So no ids are involved; the fl-id-* attributes went in FLUID-7030. The only
  landmarks are coarse:
  - The page as a whole: the document's root element, found by its location and
    fluid-site-root.
  - Islands: elements bearing fluid-layers.
  - Blocks: elements named by the linkage, data-fluid-block.

  Below those, everything is position. That's why isomorphism matters so much:
  same templates, same data, same markdown pipeline. Where they diverge, the
  claim fails and the node is replaced, as with the <h2>-inside-<p> case. It's
  also why a booted page costs real work: the template activation and one
  comparing pass over the DOM, about 1.7 s for a whole page, including loading.
  The saving is in not touching the DOM, not in skipping the walk.

  The page-subtree route for widget state

  I think it's workable, with one condition: the islands' paths must not change
  through the takeover.

  The arena in Infusion is a component a host nominates
  (fluid.history.arenaRoot), under which free components live as named members
  via fluid.initChildComponent, rather than straight under the global root. Your
  idea maps onto it like this:
  - Boot: instead of putting a free component per island at the root (figure-6),
    self-boot would put components under a page component, one member per
    block. The landmark is already in the static markup (data-fluid-block), and
    each block's islands become that member's children.
  - Takeover: a layer arriving on that member (ponder.content plus
    fluid.withEditing, by linkage or dynamically) rather than a new component
    grafted elsewhere.

  The REQUIREMENTS R6 experiment suggests this preserves widgets. When a linkage
  added a layer to a component, only that component's instance object turned
  over. Its children kept their instances, and unchanged $computes weren't
  re-evaluated. So a bound widget in a child island should survive, if the
  island's subcomponent record is unchanged by the takeover. That's the
  condition: the block component's verbatim rendering must allocate the same
  member names (island-1 and so on) with equivalent records, or the islands turn
  over anyway.

  Two risks to test:
  - The view re-activates: a turnover of the block member re-activates its whole
    template. The DOM is reconciled in place, but every binding effect is
    reallocated (also noted in R6).
  - Island member names: these are currently allocated by order
    (allocateJointName). Block-level booting must name islands the same way as
    the content component will, or use stable names such as fluid-id.

  It's worth an experiment before committing to it.

❯ What I had imagined when I pointed you at the "Build systems" paper is that   
  the reactive work of producing the tree would itself be memoised, and it      
  would be possible to prove, perhaps by having taken some hash over subtrees   
  in the dom, or having stored trace info off to the side, that given DOM nodes 
  were definitely the output of a particular rendering process and no further   
  work was required. But I guess thinking in detail this is naive - the work of 
  constructing the component tree has to be done one way or the other, and the  
  DOM is in any case a disorderly environment where nodes could come and go     
  without formality, this is not like a build system where a timestamp or hash  
  can be put alongside an artefact and stay put. So what I'm wondering is why   
  is there some good reason why the process of booting against a page should    
  take so substantially longer than hydrating its markup in the first place,    
  which looks like it involves exactly the same work? The build system is slow  
  but not that slow, and I believe it can render the entire site comfortably in 
  less than 1.7 seconds, let alone one single page. Could you make a rough      
  guess why this process costs so much more than expected?                      

● My best guess is that most of the 1.7 s is my measurement, not Infusion. The
  boot experiment's timer runs across a fixed 1.5-second sleep I put in to let
  late SFC loads settle. That leaves roughly 200 ms of real work, which would
  match what you'd expect next to the build. I'll check by timing the first
  settle on its own:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● You were right to doubt it: the 1.7 s was my measurement, not Infusion. A
  whole page actually boots in about 230 ms.

  My experiment started its timer before booting, then deliberately slept 1.5
  seconds before taking its final reading, to let any late SFC loads settle.
  That sleep was inside the timed span. Timing the first settle on its own:

  ┌───────────────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     Page      │ Settled in │ Identical to the static page at that point │
  ├───────────────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ A single post │ 229 ms     │ yes                                        │
  ├───────────────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ /post/ list   │ 235 ms     │ yes                                        │
  ├───────────────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Home page     │ 237 ms     │ yes                                        │
  └───────────────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  These 230 ms don't include loading Infusion's own files, which happens before
  the timer starts.

  Why it's still more than the build's share per page. The build renders all 67
  pages in about 2.8 s, roughly 40 ms each. But it pays its fixed costs once for
  the whole site, and the client pays them for a single page. The two fixed
  costs:

  - Fetching and parsing every SFC. The whole-page boot imports all of
    site.html's 60 or so SFCs, and each is fetched, then parsed with lezer. I'd
    guess this is most of the 230 ms. Importing only the SFCs a page's
    components use would cut it. The trace could list them per page, since its
    layer and template inputs are exactly that set.
  - Building the component tree and activating every template.

  Reconciling against the static markup is probably a small part, since claimed
  nodes are reused and attributes written only where they differ. That's a
  guess; I haven't profiled the split.

  On the memoisation question, I agree with your conclusion. The DOM can't carry
  a proof that sits still the way a build artefact's hash does, and the
  component tree must be built either way, because it's what makes the page
  live. What the trace can still do on the client is shrink the work rather than
  skip it: it can tell the client which SFCs, layers and model values a page
  needs, so it loads no more than that.

● Starting with the page-subtree experiment. The question it has to answer is
  whether a widget island's component survives when the component holding it
  gains layers dynamically. If it does, the "takeover" can be an adaptation of a
  page-level component rather than a regraft.

  that "the widget restarted" becomes a number. Three scenarios, in a real
  browser:
  - A, as now: a free island at the root, then a block component taking over.
  - B, the page subtree: the block's component lives under a page component and
    holds its islands from the start; the takeover then adds the editing layers
    dynamically.
  - C, an edit: in B, the block's text changes but its islands don't.

● All three are done. Widgets now survive the start of editing, the extension's
  late-boot workaround is gone, and the extension migrates pages by booting them
  whole. Nothing is committed.

  1. Page-subtree experiment. Your idea works. I gave a widget island a counter
  for how often its $bindable binds and unbinds, then compared two arrangements:

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────┬────────────────┐
  │                  Arrangement                   │ Binds │    Unbinds     │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────┤
  │ Free island at the root, then a block          │ 2     │ 1 (the widget  │
  │ component takes over (as before)               │       │ restarted)     │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────┼────────────────┤
  │ Island as a child of a block component from    │       │                │
  │ the start; the block then gains editing        │ 1     │ 0              │
  │ layers, changes its view's template, and is    │       │                │
  │ edited                                         │       │                │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────┴────────────────┘

  The block component itself turns over when it gains layers, but its island
  children don't. The "page" component is simply the document component of the
  page's own tree, so whole-page boot and widget preservation turned out to be
  the same change.

  2. Late-boot workaround removed. Following last round's reordering, the bridge
  now declares modules and imports before loading Infusion, and Infusion picks
  them up as it boots.

  3. Whole pages:
  - Static visits: a page with live widgets is now marked fluid-page-boot on its
    root element, a new Infusion attribute that stops self-boot booting its
    elements alone. It boots its whole tree from its model slice, through a new
    site script, ponder/infusion/js/pageBoot.js. The widgets then run as
    children of the content's components, with no free components anywhere.
    Pages without widgets still load no Infusion.
  - Editing: the extension reuses a page that booted itself, or boots it whole
    first. It then adds fluid.withEditing to the components that already render
    the blocks. withEditing now leaves the block's own html alone and renders an
    editedHtml in its place.
  - One fix along the way: on a page the extension boots itself, the page's
    first render was removing the extension's editor panel, which was already in
    the page. The bridge now takes its own nodes out during that first render
    and puts them back afterwards.

  Results: the end-to-end test passes on four pages.
  - Stabilization post: the widget's DOM is the same nodes after migration, so
    it wasn't restarted.
  - Reactivity post: the visualiser is live after migration, but I couldn't
    check it wasn't restarted there. My test has to reload that page to migrate
    it (its source differs from GitHub's), which leaves nothing to compare
    against.
  - Plain and figure posts: the migrated blocks are identical to the build's
    output.

  npm test gives 2433/2436 and the Chromium suite 393/395, both failing only the
  known tldraw tests. The trace test passes and lint is clean.

  Still open:
  - Unmeasured cost: pages with widgets now load all of the site's 60 or so
    SFCs. I expect it's a real cost but haven't measured it; the trace could
    narrow the list to the SFCs each page actually uses.
  - Fallback path: pages that can't migrate still use the preview path with its
    island-filling workaround.
  - From before: the 404 emoji, the title-edit imprecision, skipping unchanged
    pages in the build, and a real commit against a test branch.

  the whole idiom of the <fluid-import mechanism? Ensure that this is so. What

● On the first question: yes, that's the idiom. A page imports the root of its
  tree, and each SFC imports what it needs with its own top-level
  <fluid-import>. Two things are in the way here. site.html lists every SFC by
  hand, which REQUIREMENTS R15 already flags as provisional. And many of
  ponder's layers are chosen by name at runtime, such as ponder.kind.page or the
  adapt/ features, so no static import can name them. The decisive question is
  whether declaring an import fetches the SFC, or only maps its layer to a path
  until something demands it. Checking loadImportMap:

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)
● The loader currently starts fetching every declared SFC at once, so I'll make
  imports lazy: register paths at declaration and load each layer only when it's
  demanded. One function defined in one SFC and called from another,
  ponder.relatedPosts.index from ponder.site, would lose that guarantee, so I'm
  moving it into the site's SFC and reading ensureImportsLoaded first. · summary

         -class="post-entry"><div>The term glitch in the sense of a react

         -Gabriel the finest writer on software technology of his generat
         -ion. Connecting this idea with Christopher Alexander’s idea of 
         -organic growth in the context of the architecture of buildings,
         - Gabriel says Habitability is the characteristic of source code
         - that enables programmers, coders, bug-fixers, and people comin
         -g to the code later in its life to understand its construction

● Both runs give identical results, 22 steps passed and 12 failed, so the tldraw
  demo failures predate lazy loading (most likely the same breakage behind the
  tldraw unit-test failures). The compose-edit demo passes either way. The lazy
  Fluid.js is restored.

  Yes, that's the idiom, and it is now how pages load. Infusion was loading
  every declared SFC eagerly, though its own TODO said loading should wait until
  a layer is demanded. I've made that change, so declaring an import now costs
  nothing until something uses its layer, and site.html's full list is harmless.
  A whole-booted post now fetches 31 of the site's 66 SFCs: the 26 layers its
  trace records, plus the site's feature holders, which the site tree demands on
  every page. Nothing is committed.

  Infusion changes:
  - loadImportMap only registers each layer's file. A new fluid.loadImport
    starts the load, once, when the layer is demanded by ensureImportsLoaded or
    subscribeDocToInjections.
  - On the server, a free component has no document of its own, so an import now
    remembers the document that declared it and injects into that. Without
    this, the build deadlocked.
  - A new test checks that a declared but undemanded import loads nothing.

  ponder changes:
  - Functions moved to the SFCs that call them. A function defined in one SFC
    and called from another's template or $compute is no longer guaranteed to be
    loaded in time. A scan found two such cases: relatedIndex moved into
    ponder-site.vue, and hasPager into ponder-main.vue. The other cross-SFC
    calls go to the site's root SFC, which always loads first.
  - Each page's slice now lists the layers that rendered it, and pageBoot.js
    loads exactly those SFCs before building the page's tree. Without that, the
    tree rendered while layers were still loading, then re-rendered and replaced
    the content block's element, which broke the editor's state labels and
    could flash for a visitor. The block element is now kept.
  - Failed builds no longer prune. A build that fails to render every page no
    longer writes traces or removes pages as "stale". One of my failed builds
    had emptied docs/ that way before I rebuilt it.

  Checks:
  - Builds: eager and lazy builds of all 70 pages are identical apart from
    attribute order.
  - Extension: the end-to-end tests pass on all four pages, with the widget's
    DOM preserved through migration.
  - Suites: npm test gives 2439/2442 and the browser suite 394/396, failing only
    the known tldraw tests. The trace, output-documents and hydrate tests pass,
    and lint is clean.
  - Demos: the tldraw demo fails 12 of 34 steps with eager and lazy loading
    alike, so that predates this change. The compose-edit demo passes.

  Pages that can't migrate:
  - Pages without the build's metadata: another site's pages, pages built before
    this work, and pages with no slice. The extension needs a linkage record
    naming Infusion, the SFCs and a model slice, and alias redirect pages don't
    get one.
  - Pages holding a different Infusion: for instance, third-party embeds or a
    stale vendored copy, as the reactivity post had before this round.
    Infusion's files can be evaluated only once per page, so the extension falls
    back to its preview path.
  - Pages whose security policy forbids inline scripts: injecting an SFC's
    script needs 'unsafe-inline' or equivalent. GitHub Pages sets no such
    policy; many sites do.
  - Pages served from file://: fetching the slice or SFCs fails in most
    browsers.
  - Pages whose markup isn't what their tree would render: a stale docs/ built
    from older content or SFCs, or HTML edited by hand after the build. These
    still migrate, but the first render replaces what differs instead of
    claiming it, and edits are based on the repository's current source.
  - Pages whose content still has script-filled DOM, like the 404 emoji. They
    migrate, but booting clears what the script added.

● I've added the note as section 3.5, "Pages which can't be migrated", in
  a-scratch/reports/0-live-static-editing.md, at the end of the architecture
  section and just before the work list.

  It opens by saying what migration depends on, the page's linkage record and
  its model slice, and that the extension falls back to its preview path when a
  page can't be migrated. It then covers the six kinds of page from my last
  answer:

  - Missing build metadata: another site's pages, older builds, and pages with
    no slice, such as alias redirects.
  - A different Infusion on the page: for example a third-party embed or a stale
    vendored copy. A page running the copy the site publishes is reused
    instead.
  - A security policy forbidding inline scripts: an SFC's script is injected
    inline.
  - Pages served from file://: the slice and SFC fetches fail.
  - Markup that isn't what the page's tree renders: stale or hand-edited HTML.
    These migrate, but the first render replaces what differs.
  - Content holding DOM a page script fills in: for example the 404 emoji. These
    migrate, but booting clears what the script wrote; such material should
    become a component, as the two widgets did.

● The tldraw demo was broken by my change from earlier today making imports
  lazy. It's now fixed, and the demo passes all 14 of its steps.

  What went wrong. The demo's layer picker lists the widget layers that have
  been defined. Its widgets are declared with ordinary <fluid-import>s, and
  under lazy loading nothing demanded them until a widget was created, so the
  picker was empty. Every step that needs a widget then failed.

  My earlier "eager" comparison failed the same way, which misled me into
  thinking the failures predated the change. That patch fetched each SFC but
  never injected it into the page: injection used to happen through a
  subscription made for every import, and I had removed it as part of the
  lazy-loading change. I confirmed the cause by running the demo against the
  committed code in a scratch copy, where it passed 14 of 14, and then swapping
  in my changed files one at a time.

  The fix. A page can now mark a <fluid-import> as eager, so it is loaded and
  injected at once, without waiting for something to demand its layer. The
  tldraw demo marks its nine palette imports so, with a comment saying why.
  Ordinary pages keep loading only what they use. The change is in FluidView.js
  and demo/tldraw/index.html.

  Checks:
  - Demos: npm run test:browser passes all 34 steps across both demos.
  - Tests: npm test gives 2439/2442 and the browser suite 394/396. The failures
    are the three "Ask me anything" tests (two in the browser suite), which were
    already failing when this session began.
  - Lint: clean.

  The published copy of the demo, docs/demo/tldraw/index.html, still has the old
  imports, so it will lack the eager markers until you regenerate docs/ with
  build.js. The "Ask me anything" failures look like a separate issue, possibly
  expectations left behind by yesterday's switch to the new Cloudflare proxies;
  I haven't investigated them.

❯ OK - let's start sketching out the bidirectional editing scheme. My rough     
  research suggests that we may not get away without using both ProseMirror and 
  CodeMirror-markdown, if we want both representations to be straightforwardly  
  editable. I got away with simple content-editable in my rough demo but that   
  isn't going to fly for anything else. I'm worried about the dependency burden 
  people will accept all kinds of stuff happening in edit mode. Is it possible  
  to imagine that a ProseMirror "adoption" could happen isomorphically or       
  might we simply have to "roll our own" rich text editing experience? Can you  
  think of a reasonable experience that avoids having both dependencies?        

● Yes: I think there's a reasonable experience that avoids needing both, and a
  ProseMirror adoption could be made to work isomorphically, with real caveats.
  Neither cost lands on readers, though: the editing SFCs load only once
  fluid.withEditing is demanded, now that imports are lazy. So the dependency
  burden is on editors, who tolerate more.

  Can ProseMirror adopt a page isomorphically?

  Partly, and the conditions are telling.

  - Adoption. ProseMirror can build its document from existing DOM
    (DOMParser.fromSchema(schema).parse(element)), so it can take over a block
    as published without the markdown source. But its editor view then owns that
    element's subtree and re-renders it from its own schema's toDOM. The nodes
    are replaced, though they'd look the same if toDOM matches the build's HTML.
  - Islands. Shortcodes would be ProseMirror node views, which can adopt an
    existing element as their DOM. So a widget island could survive, as the
    page-subtree experiment showed for Infusion.
  - Isomorphism means two renderers agreeing. The build renders with
    markdown-it; ProseMirror renders with its schema. Keeping them identical is
    the same discipline as the shared markdown pipeline, verifiable with a test
    like the isomorphism check over all 49 files. Usefully, prosemirror-markdown
    parses with markdown-it, our tokeniser. But each of our extensions needs a
    schema entry and a serializer rule: attributes {.class}, footnotes,
    definition lists, heading anchors, highlighted fences, islands.
  - Two models fighting over one subtree. While ProseMirror is mounted,
    Infusion's content component must stop rendering that block
    (fluid.disableRendering exists for exactly this), and edits flow back as
    markdown into editSource.
  - Fidelity. ProseMirror's markdown serializer normalises: list markers,
    emphasis style, line wrapping, escaping. Serialising the whole document
    after a one-word edit produces noisy diffs. That's tolerable for a commit,
    but unpleasant for anyone reviewing the markdown.

  So: workable, but it's a second rendering pipeline to keep isomorphic, plus a
  mode where Infusion steps aside.

  The two-dependency worry

  You need both libraries only if you want two simultaneous, equally polished 
  representations. The alternatives each pick one representation as the truth:

  1. CodeMirror 6 only, "live preview" (Obsidian's model). Markdown text stays
     the single source of truth. Decorations hide the syntax and render
     headings, emphasis, links and images in place, with widgets for islands.
     Bidirectionality is trivially exact, since there is only one document;
     there's nothing to round-trip. The cost is that structural editing (lists,
     tables) still feels source-like, and it isn't true WYSIWYG for people who
     never want to see a #. Infusion ships CodeMirror 5, but live preview really
     needs CodeMirror 6's decoration model, so it's a new dependency.
  2. ProseMirror only, with source as a per-block mode. Rich editing is the
     default; "edit source" turns one block into a code block, or a plain
     textarea, holding that block's markdown. You lose syntax highlighting in
     source mode unless you keep the CodeMirror 5 Infusion already has, which
     isn't a new dependency.
  3. Roll our own, block-structured (the Editor.js / Notion model). This is the
     one I'd recommend exploring first, because it matches what you already need
     for the block palette:
     - The content is segmented into top-level markdown blocks, each keeping its
       source span; markdown-it's tokens record their line ranges (token.map).
       Each block is an Infusion component.
     - A paragraph, heading or list item is edited inline with contenteditable,
       restricted to inline marks (bold, italic, code, link). Input is handled
       with beforeinput events rather than letting the browser invent markup. A
       small serializer turns that block's inline DOM back into markdown.
     - Only the edited block is re-serialised and spliced into the original
       source. Every other byte is untouched, which solves the diff problem
       outright (research item R4 in the plan).
     - Structure is never edited by the browser: adding, removing, splitting,
       merging and reordering blocks are the palette's and the components' job.
       Islands are just blocks.
     - Any block can flip to its source, using the CodeMirror 5 Infusion already
       ships, or a textarea. A whole-document source view is the same thing at
       page scale.

     This keeps the genuinely hard parts of rich-text editing small: selection
     never crosses blocks, and IME, undo and paste are handled one block at a
     time. It's what your rough demo did, with the boundary drawn at the block,
     which is where contenteditable stops being dangerous. What it doesn't do
     well: rich structures inside a block, such as nested lists edited fluidly
     and tables. Those could later get a specialised editor, and ProseMirror for
     just those block kinds would be a contained use of it.

  My suggestion

  Start with option 3, with source mode on the existing CodeMirror 5, so there
  is no new dependency.
  - Whole-document markdown editing is CodeMirror 5, exact by construction.
  - Rich editing is per-block inline editing, exact everywhere except the blocks
    you touch, and minimal even there.
  - ProseMirror stays an option for complex block types, adopted per block
    rather than per page.

  The first experiment I'd propose is the block segmentation itself. Split each
  content file into blocks with source spans, render each as a component, and
  check that the page is still byte-identical to the build. That's the
  precondition for every option above except the CodeMirror 6 one, and it's
  measurable today.

  of the existing compose-edit demo. Story that should work: User goes          
  activates the extension to go into edit mode, then triggers a further control 
  that says "also edit framing" - this makes the entirety of the view           
  editable, including material such as headers/footers and even stuff derived   
  from config that used to be in hugo.yaml. The user edits part of a footer -   
  this gets committed to IndexedDB - they then browse to another page on the    
  site, they see their footer edit on that page also, highlighted in the same   
  "this is edited but not committed" frame that they saw before, until the true 
  rebuild happens. Check that this scenario is workable within the structure    
  we already have and write a test based on it. It occurs to me that the        
  testability aspect of this whole infrastructure needs separate work, and we   
  will need a kind of a "mock GitHub" that will simulate the kinds of bulk      
  build via Actions and Content API interactions. Start building such a         
  framework and starting issuing a few scenario tests like this against it.

● The framing scenario works with the structure we already had, and its test
  passes against a new mock GitHub: 16 of 16 checks. Before your message came
  in, I'd finished the block-segmentation experiment. The pell-style editor
  recast hasn't been started.

  Block segmentation (ponder infusion/js/markdown.js)

  - ponderMarkdown.segment(md, body) parses the whole document once and renders
    each top-level block from its share of the parsed result, using the whole
    document's state. Heading ids, footnotes and reference links therefore come
    out as in a whole-page render.
    - Each block records its kind and its line range in the source.
    - Raw HTML that opens in one block and closes in a later one is merged into
      a single block. So are comment-only blocks.
    - Footnote definitions belong to the footnotes block.
    - Multi-line shortcodes now expand with padding, so line numbers still match
      the source.
  - Results over all 49 content files:
    - Joining the block renderings gives exactly the whole-page render.
    - Every non-blank source line falls in exactly one block, in order.
    - In the browser, rendering the blocks as a component list produces DOM
      identical to the whole page, and all 8 islands are owned by their blocks.
  - Two Infusion fixes (FluidView.js) were needed for that: a template whose
    root is <fluid-fragment> now renders, and verbatim list members insert their
    nodes directly with no wrapper element.
  - Build fix: the build now records what it writes into each page after
    rendering (linkage record, boot scripts) as an input in the page traces.
    Before, changing that material didn't count as a change, so pages weren't
    rewritten.

  Editing framing

  - Linkage: ponder's infusion/linkage.json now declares framing: the footer and
    navbar SFCs, each with its layer. Every page's linkage record lists them,
    and their hashes go into the trace's sources, so publication is detected the
    same way as for content.
  - Extension:
    - "Also edit framing" boots the whole page, outlines the framing as
      editable, and adds a picker so the panel can switch between the page's
      content and its framing sources.
    - A framing edit is an ordinary IndexedDB claim. It is applied through
      fluid.loadSFCText, so every footer re-renders from it.
    - It is marked with attributes only, labelled through CSS, so re-rendering
      doesn't remove the marking.
    - Pages with no source of their own, such as lists, now start the extension
      and show framing claims.
    - Polling re-reads each claim from the service worker, because the commit
      may have been made from another tab. That gap was the one failure in the
      first run.

  Mock GitHub (extension/test/)

  - mock-github.js: copies the site into a scratch repository and serves:
    - the Contents API, returning real git blob shas and 409 on a stale sha;
    - Actions, which run ponder's own build after a delay, one at a time;
    - Pages, serving the built site.
  - harness.js: launches Chromium with the extension pointed at the mock, and
    provides scenario helpers.
  - framing-scenario.js (npm run test:extension) checks:
    a. The footer is edited on a post and is marked uncommitted there.
    b. A list page shows the edit with the same marking, while the published
       list page is unchanged.
    c. After commit, the rebuild publishes the edit, and the list page drops the
       claim and reloads to the published footer.
    d. A content edit committed after someone else changed the file ends up in
       conflict.

  npm test (2442/2442) and the browser suite (396/396) still pass after the
  Infusion changes.

  What's missing

  - Config isn't framing yet. Making hugo.toml editable needs a TOML parser in
    the browser and a way to feed the parsed config into the page's live state.
  - Framing is edited as SFC source in the panel, not by typing into the page as
    in the compose-edit demo.
  - A page only polls claims it already knew about when it loaded. One made
    later in another tab isn't picked up until reload.

  I've added these notes as section 3.6 of
  a-scratch/reports/0-live-static-editing.md. Next is the pell-style mixin:
  editable blocks, an inline DOM→markdown serializer, and a source view.

      536 +                                                              
      537 +## 3.7 wend.json, and the block editor (2026-11-19)           
      538 +                                                              
      539 +**wend.json** replaces ponder's hugo.toml. It is a *patch* of 
          +the members of the root of the site's tree, `ponder.site`,    
      540 +applied when it is constructed (`siteModel.patchOptions`; page
          +Boot.js alike, from the page's model slice, which now         
      541 +carries the whole `patch`): `config` - title, baseURL, mainSec
          +tions, author, menu, params - and `features`, the switches    
      542 +of the site's optional features (`selfHosted`, `hljs`), which 
          +`ponder.site`'s `$if`s now read. Each member of plain data    
      543 +becomes a reactive root, so reads of it are traced; a member h
          +olding Infusion syntax, e.g. a `$component` record, would     
      544 +pass as it is - the place for a component's own options, e.g. 
          +a highlighter's, rather than amongst the site's params.       
      545 +Dropped as Hugo's alone or unused: theme, publishDir, relative
          +URLs, pygments*, goldmark, Services (Disqus, Google           
      546 +Analytics), delayDisqus, readingTime, wordCount, rss, commit, 
          +cusdis, and the author's placeholder social handles (the      
      547 +media icons are written out in their SFC). Every page and feed
          + builds identically, hashes aside. wend.json is framing of    
      548 +kind "patch": the extension applies an edit of it by setting t
          +he root's members (`setPatch`), so e.g. the footer's          
      549 +author re-renders live (tested in framing-scenario.js).       
      550 +                                                              
      551 +**The block editor** (`extension/edit-in-infusion/sfc/fluid-bl
          +ockEditor.vue`, layer `fluid.blockEditor`, broadcast with     
      552 +fluid.withEditing onto the content block's component) - a succ
          +essor of the pell-edit demo, without execCommand:             
      553 + - the source is segmented by the site's own pipeline (`ponder
          +Markdown.segment`); each block whose rendering the            
      554 +   serialiser (`js/fluid-markdownSerializer.js`) reproduces - 
          +checked per block, as DOM, by rendering its serialisation     
      555 +   (`roundTrips`) - is contenteditable in place; the rest (fen
          +ces, tables, islands, raw HTML, footnote references) are      
      556 +   marked as edited through the source. Over ponder's corpus 1
          +301 of 1332 such blocks round-trip                            
      557 + - leaving an edited block serialises it, and splices it into 
          +the source in place of its own lines alone - re-wrapped       
      558 +   at the width its source was wrapped at - and the source is 
          +announced to the extension, which holds it as the claim       
      559 +   and renders it as any edit, so what is shown is always the 
          +site's own rendering of the markdown                          
      560 + - a floating toolbar (kind of block: text, headings, quotatio
          +n, lists; bold, italic, code, link) and keys (Ctrl+B/I/E);

● hugo.toml is now wend.json, and the pell-style block editor works in the page.
  Both mock-GitHub scenarios pass from fresh builds: framing 19/19 and the
  block editor 16/16. I didn't re-run the Infusion core suites after these
  changes; none of today's edits touch core.

  wend.json (ponder)

  - It's a patch on ponder.site's members, applied at construction in both the
    build and in-browser page boot. Each member holding plain data becomes
    reactive state, so reads of it are traced and in-browser edits update the
    page.
    - config holds the title, baseURL, mainSections, author, menu and the
      remaining params.
    - features holds the switches selfHosted and hljs, which the feature
      components now read in place of the old params.
    - A member written in Infusion syntax (e.g. a $component record) passes
      through unchanged. That is where a component's own options, such as a
      highlighter's, would go in future.
  - Removed:
    - Hugo-only settings: theme, publishDir, relativeURLs, pygments, goldmark.
    - Disqus and Google Analytics.
    - Unused params: delayDisqus, readingTime, wordCount, rss, commit, cusdis.
    - The author's placeholder "username" social handles.
  - Every page and feed builds identically to before, apart from hashes.
  - wend.json is now editable framing. Changing the author's name in it
    re-renders the footer live; the framing scenario checks this.
  - hugo.toml is deleted from the working tree; a copy is in
    /tmp/claude-1000/-home-amb26-Source-gits-infusion-6/0ad89a03-cfb6-47ba-86e1-
    98ee818f2f6e/scratchpad/hugo.toml.bak.
  - smol-toml is now unused, but I left it in package.json. Removing it there
    alone would put the lockfile out of sync and break npm ci, so drop it with
    an npm uninstall when convenient.

  Block editor (extension/edit-in-infusion/sfc/fluid-blockEditor.vue)

  It's an SFC mixin (fluid.blockEditor), added to the content block's component
  alongside fluid.withEditing. It uses neither execCommand nor any library.

  - Which blocks are editable: each block is checked by turning it into markdown
    and rendering that back with the site's pipeline. If the result matches
    what's on the page, the block is editable in place; if not, it is marked as
    source-only, so editing in the page can't silently lose anything. Over the
    whole corpus, 1301 of 1332 paragraphs, headings, lists and quotations pass.
    The rest contain footnote references or raw HTML. Code blocks, tables and
    islands are always source-only.
  - Edits replace only the block's own lines. When you leave an edited block, it
    is turned back into markdown and replaces just its own lines in the source,
    re-wrapped at the width the source used. Every other block's source stays
    exactly as written. The page is then re-rendered from the source by the
    site's own pipeline.
  - The toolbar sits over the block in hand. It offers a block-type menu (text,
    headings, quotation, lists), plus bold, italic, code and link (Ctrl+B /
    Ctrl+I / Ctrl+E). Enter splits a paragraph and moves the caret into the new
    one; Backspace at the start of a block joins it to the previous one; paste
    inserts plain text.
  - For people who never want to see a #: the markdown source is folded away and
    the panel shrinks to a small card. Unfold "Markdown source" to see or edit
    the markdown beside the page.

  Testing

  - The test support grew a little: MOCK_GITHUB_REUSE=../ponder/docs reuses an
    already-built site, which saves a build while developing a scenario. npm run
    test:extension runs both scenarios.
  - Not covered by tests yet: the link button and Backspace-joining. The
    screenshot check only confirmed the toolbar and the editing highlight render
    properly.

  Technology choice

  Inline editing has no library. Editing blocks one at a time keeps the
  browser's contenteditable well-behaved, and the round-trip check guards
  correctness. For the source view I'd recommend CodeMirror 6 next, with the
  block being edited highlighted. ProseMirror or TipTap would bring their own
  document model, which would compete with the site's markdown being the single
  source of truth.

  Next steps

  These are noted in section 3.7 of the working doc:
  - a block palette for inserting new blocks, including islands;
  - list items treated as blocks of their own;
  - editing footnotes in place;
  - showing why a block can only be edited as source.

● The CodeMirror 6 source view is in place of the panel's textarea. Both
  scenarios pass from fresh builds: framing 19/19, block editor 20/20, including
  two new source-view steps.

  What it does (extension/edit-in-infusion/js/sourceView.js)
  - Languages: chosen from the file's path: Markdown for content, Vue for
    framing SFCs, JSON for wend.json. It also has line numbers, undo history,
    search and line wrapping.
  - Linked to the page: focusing a block in the page highlights its lines in the
    source and scrolls to them. Putting the cursor in the source marks the
    matching block in the page and scrolls it into view.
  - Side by side: when the source is unfolded, the page shifts left to make room
    for the panel. Folded, the panel stays a small card for people who don't
    want to see markdown.
  - Cursor and undo survive in-page edits: an edit made in the page reaches the
    editor as only the changed span, not a full replacement.

  How it's packaged
  - A Manifest V3 extension can't load remote code, so CodeMirror is vendored as
    one bundle, edit-in-infusion/lib/codemirror6.js (~550 KB). Most of that is
    the Vue support's HTML/CSS/JS grammars.
  - extension/codemirror/ builds it with esbuild and has its own package.json.
    Rebuild with npm install && npm run build there.
  - I ran npm install there, which downloaded the packages from the npm
    registry. Its node_modules is gitignored; its package-lock.json is new.
  - The bundle loads as a content script on every http(s) page, before edit.js.
    If parsing it everywhere is too costly, the alternative is injecting it on
    activation, which needs the scripting permission.

  Two problems found along the way
  - Blank editor: CodeMirror puts its styles in a <style> tag in <head>, and the
    page's component tree removed it when it booted. The tag is now marked as
    the extension's own, and the bridge already keeps such elements safe while
    the page boots.
  - Unbounded height: flex layout doesn't reach inside <details>, so the editor
    grew to the full document height. It now has an explicit height, and
    re-measures when the source is unfolded.

  Testing
  - So that tests can still read and write the source, the editor's text is
    mirrored into a hidden <textarea>, and text written there counts as an edit.
  - The two new scenario steps check the line highlighting, the cursor marking
    its block, and typing in the source updating the page.

  Notes are in section 3.8 of the working doc.
