● Links now autocomplete in the markdown source editor. Both scenarios pass from
  fresh builds: framing 19/19, block editor 25/25 including the new link step.
  I checked it through tests only, not with a screenshot of the suggestion list.

  How it behaves
  - Pages: after [text](, it suggests the site's pages, showing each page's
    title next to its path. Matching is on the path as you type it, not the
    title. Extra list pages like /post/page/2/ are left out, as is the page
    you're editing.
  - Images: after ![alt](, it suggests the site's images. Paths containing
    spaces are wrapped in <...> so the markdown still works.
  - Path form: start with / (or nothing) and you get site-root paths like
    /docs/fluid-view/, which the build already turns into correct relative URLs
    on each page. Start with ./ or ../ and you get paths relative to the page
    you're editing, like ../../img/x.jpg.

  Where the suggestions come from
  - The site's published trace file, fetched once when the editor opens.
  - ponder's build now adds each page's title and kind (a single page or a list)
    to the trace, plus an assets list of the site's own linkable files from
    static/ (images and PDFs).

  Changes
  - ponder: trace.js, buildSite.js.
  - Extension:
    - sourceView.js has the completion logic.
    - edit.js loads the page list.
    - The CodeMirror bundle now includes @codemirror/autocomplete, rebuilt from
      extension/codemirror with package.json updated to match.

  Test
  Step 8 of block-editor-scenario.js covers it. Choosing a suggestion with Enter
  only works once the list has been open for 75ms (CodeMirror's guard against
  accidental Enter presses), so the test waits briefly first. Someone typing
  won't notice it.

  Not done yet
  - Completing # links to headings: the heading ids come from the markdown
    pipeline, so the trace would need to record them per page.
  - Completion inside raw-HTML href="...".
  - Completion in the link box of the in-page toolbar.

  These are in section 3.9 of the working doc.

● Links to headings now complete too. Both scenarios pass from fresh builds:
  framing 19/19, block editor 29/29.

  How it behaves
  - This page: typing [text](# lists the headings of the page you're editing.
  - Other pages: typing [text](/docs/fluid-view/# (or a relative path such as
    ../other/#) lists that page's headings.
  - The list: headings show by title, indented by level, in page order. Choosing
    one inserts the whole link, e.g. /docs/fluid-view/#a-first-component.
  - New headings work immediately: for the page you're editing, headings come
    from the source as it stands now, refreshed half a second after each change.
    So a heading you've just written, or one made in the page with the toolbar,
    can be linked to before it's published. Other pages' headings come from the
    last published build.

  Changes
  - ponder:
    - markdown.js gains ponderMarkdown.headings, which lists headings with the
      ids the site's own pipeline gives them.
    - The build's trace file now records each page's headings.
    - Because markdown.js changed, 47 pages were rebuilt.
  - Extension:
    - The bridge has a headings request that lists the live source's headings.
    - edit.js loads the site's page list once and keeps this page's headings
      current.
    - sourceView.js handles completion after #.

  headings, the unpublished subheading made in step 4, and another page's
  headings with the full link written into the source.

❯ OK - what would it take to get the Chrome extension published in the app      
  store?                                                                        

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● It's mostly packaging and policy work. The code needs one real change
  (narrowing where it runs) and two smaller ones. I checked this against the
  current manifest and code; the store details are from memory, so confirm
  current specifics (e.g. the fee) on Google's developer pages.

  Changes needed in the extension

  1. Stop running on every website. The content script currently matches
  http://*/* and https://*/*. That gives the extension access to every site the
  user visits, and loads the 550 KB CodeMirror bundle on every page. Broad
  access like this gets the strictest review, the slowest approval, and a "Read
  and change all your data on all websites" warning at install. The usual fix:
  - Use the activeTab and scripting permissions.
  - Inject the scripts only when the user clicks the extension's button.
  - Optionally, let users permanently allow particular sites they edit, through
    optional_host_permissions, so their claims still show without a click.

  As it stands, the extension finds a page's linkage record by itself and shows
  the "edited, not committed" frames automatically. After the change that would
  happen only on sites the user has allowed, which is a reasonable trade.

  2. Explain the scripts it loads into pages. MV3 bans extensions from running
  code fetched from the network. The bridge adds <script> tags to the page that
  load the site's own published Infusion and markdown pipeline. They run in the
  page's own context, not the extension's, so I think this is defensible: it's
  the site's own code, run as the site would run it. But a reviewer could flag
  it. The store submission should state it plainly, and the README should
  explain the design.

  3. Replace the pasted personal access token. Users currently paste a GitHub
  token into the options page. That works, but it's hostile to the non-technical
  audience you're aiming at, and a stored full-repo token is a liability.
  Better is GitHub's device flow or a GitHub App with access to just the
  repository. That needs a GitHub App or OAuth app registered, which is a GitHub
  action I'd need you to approve.

  Smaller items:
  - Test hook: the githubApi setting that points the extension at the mock
    GitHub should be kept out of release builds, or gated to development
    installs.
  - Icons: the manifest has none; 16, 48 and 128 px are needed.
  - Source: the vendored CodeMirror bundle is minified, which is allowed
    (obfuscation isn't), but include extension/codemirror/ so the bundle can be
    rebuilt and checked.
  - Version: bump version for each release; the current one is 0.1.0.

  Store listing and account

  - Developer account: there's a one-time registration fee (US$5 last I knew),
    2-step verification on the Google account, and a trader/non-trader
    declaration under EU rules.
  - Listing: a description, a 128 px icon, at least one 1280×800 screenshot, a
    category, and an optional promotional tile.
  - Privacy:
    - A privacy policy URL is required, since the extension handles
      authentication data (the GitHub token) and website content.
    - You also fill in the data-use disclosures. What the extension really does:
      the token stays in local extension storage, unsaved edits stay in local
      IndexedDB, and the only network traffic goes to GitHub and the site
      itself.
  - Single purpose: a statement of the extension's one purpose, plus a
    justification for each permission requested.
  - Visibility: start as unlisted, so it installs from a link but doesn't appear
    in search. That suits early users, and you can make it public later.
  - Review time: typically a few days to a few weeks. Broad host permissions and
    the script-loading question are what would slow it down.

  Suggested order

  1. Narrow where it runs (activeTab, scripting, optional per-site permission)
     and keep the mock-GitHub scenario tests passing.
  2. Gate the test hook, add icons, write the privacy policy and permission
     justifications.
  3. Publish as unlisted with the token flow as it is. Then move to device flow
     or a GitHub App before going public.

  I can do steps 1 and 2 in the code now. Registering the account, paying the
  fee, and submitting are yours to do.

       2 +<p>“Edit in Infusion” is a Chrome extension for editing a stati
         +cally published website in place, on pages which               
       3 +advertise the sources they were built from. This policy describ
         +es what it handles, where that is kept, and where it           
       4 +is sent. In short: it has no server of its own, collects nothin
         +g about you, and sends what you edit only to the               
       5 +GitHub repository of the site you are editing, when you ask it 
         +to.</p>                                                        
       6 +<h3 id="when-it-does-anything"><a href="#when-it-does-anything"
         + aria-label="When it does anything" class="infusion-docs-anchor
         +"><span aria-hidden="true" class="octicon octicon-link"></span>
         +</a>When it does anything</h3>                                 
       7 +<p>The extension does nothing on a website until you click its 
         +button there. Clicking asks your permission to access          
       8 +that site. If you grant it, the extension runs on that site’s p
         +ages from then on, so that they can show edits you             
       9 +have made which are not yet published. You can withdraw that ac
         +cess at any time from the extension’s options page,            
      10 +or from Chrome’s own extension settings. On every other site, i
         +t does nothing.</p>                                            
      11 +<h3 id="what-it-handles"><a href="#what-it-handles" aria-label=
         +"What it handles" class="infusion-docs-anchor"><span aria-hidde
         +n="true" class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>What it handle
         +s</h3>                                                         
      12 +<ul>                                                           
      13 +<li><strong>The pages of sites you enable it on.</strong> It re
         +ads the page’s <em>linkage record</em>, a small description the
         + site                                                          
      14 +publishes of the files the page was built from, and the content
         + of the page, in order to show your edits in it. It            
      15 +does not read or record anything else about your browsing.</li>
      16 +<li><strong>Your edits.</strong> The text of the files you edit
         +, held until they are published.</li>                          
      17 +<li><strong>A GitHub access token</strong> which you provide, s
         +o that it can read and commit the site’s files on your behalf.<
         +/li>                                                           
      18 +</ul>                                                          
      19 +<h3 id="where-it-is-kept"><a href="#where-it-is-kept" aria-labe
         +l="Where it is kept" class="infusion-docs-anchor"><span aria-hi
         +dden="true" class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>Where it is
         + kept</h3>                                                     
      20 +<p>Everything is kept in your own browser, in the extension’s p
         +rivate storage:</p>                                            
      21 +<ul>                                                           
      22 +<li>Your GitHub token is kept in the extension’s local storage.
         + It is never made visible to the pages you edit.</li>          
      23 +<li>Your edits are kept in the extension’s IndexedDB storage un
         +til the site is seen to have published them, or you            
      24 +discard them.</li>                                             
      25 +</ul>                                                          
      26 +<p>The extension has no server of its own and no analytics. Not
         +hing is synchronised between your devices.</p>                 
      27 +<h3 id="where-it-is-sent"><a href="#where-it-is-sent" aria-labe
         +l="Where it is sent" class="infusion-docs-anchor"><span aria-hi
         +dden="true" class="octicon octicon-link"></span></a>Where it is
         + sent</h3>                                                     
      28 +<ul>                                                           
      29 +<li><strong>To GitHub</strong> (<a href="http://api.github.com"
         +>api.github.com</a>), using your token: requests to read the fi

      30 +only when you press <em>Commit</em>, a commit of your edit to t

      31 +<a href="https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policie
         +s/github-general-privacy-statement">GitHub’s privacy statement<
         +/a>.                                                           
      32 +A commit is public if the repository is, and records your GitHu
         +b identity as its author.</li>                                 
      33 +<li><strong>To the site you are editing</strong>: requests for

      34 +build, the code it renders its pages with, and the data of the 
         +page being edited - in the same way that viewing               
      35 +the site does.</li>                                            
      36 +</ul>                                                          
      37 +<p>Nothing is sent anywhere else, and nothing is sold or shared

      39 +<p>Choosing <em>Forget token</em> in the extension’s options re

      40 +the extension removes everything it has stored.</p>

● The extension now does nothing on any site until its button is clicked. Icons,
  a privacy policy page on ponder and the store paperwork are done. Both
  scenarios pass: framing 21/21 (fresh build), block editor 29/29. The block
  editor failed once on the step where a cursor in the source marks its block in
  the page; I fixed the likely cause and it then passed three runs out of
  three.

  Do you need both a GitHub App and an OAuth Cloudflare Worker?

  No — just one GitHub App, no Worker. Curation needs its Worker because a web
  page can't keep a client secret, and GitHub's normal browser sign-in needs
  one. The extension can use GitHub's device flow instead, which needs only the
  app's client id:
  1. The extension shows a short code.
  2. The user enters it at github.com/login/device.
  3. The extension's background script picks up the token.

  The new App needs:
  - device flow switched on;
  - Contents: read and write permission;
  - installation on each site repository;
  - user tokens set not to expire, because renewing a GitHub App user token
    needs the client secret.

  Don't reuse the curation App: it only has access to Discussions and shouldn't
  gain write access to repository contents. Registering the App is a GitHub
  action for you; I can then write the sign-in flow against its client id. The
  reasoning is in section 3.10 of the working doc.

  Click-only activation

  - Manifest: it no longer runs a script on every page. It asks for activeTab
    and scripting, and lists access to http/https sites as optional, granted one
    site at a time.
  - First click on a site: it asks for access to that site. If granted, it
    enlists the site: from then on every page of that site shows your
    unpublished edits without a click. Then it opens the editor.
  - If access is declined: it still edits the current page, using the temporary
    access the click itself gives.
  - Options page: lists enlisted sites, each with a Forget button that
    unregisters the site and withdraws its access.
  - Test hooks: the mock-GitHub address and the fast polling setting now only
    work in a test build. The release build ignores them.
  - Tests:
    - Puppeteer can't click the extension button, so the test harness loads a
      copy of the extension with a test flag and the mock's address pre-allowed.
    - The framing scenario now checks that nothing is enlisted before the first
      click and that the click enlists the site.
    - The step where a later page shows the footer edit without a click now
      exercises enlistment.

  Icons

  16, 32, 48 and 128 px are in extension/edit-in-infusion/icons/, cropped from
  infusion-logo.png with its transparency kept. They're used for the toolbar
  button, the extensions page and the options page.

  Privacy policy (ponder)

● I wrote extension/test/demo.js for this. It passes lint and a syntax check,
  but I haven't run it, because it opens a window and waits for you to close it.
  Your WSL session has a display, so the window should appear on your desktop.

  Starting it
  From the infusion-6 directory:
  ! node extension/test/demo.js
  - It builds ponder into a scratch "repository" served by the mock GitHub,
    which takes about a minute.
  - To skip that build and start from ponder's current docs/, run
    MOCK_GITHUB_REUSE=../ponder/docs node extension/test/demo.js instead.
    Rebuild ponder first if its content has changed.
  - To open a different page, pass its path, e.g. node extension/test/demo.js 
    post/.

  It opens a visible Chromium at roughly 1280×800, with the extension loaded and
  already holding a fake token, on the "UI as code" post.

  Using it
  1. Pin the extension: open the puzzle-piece menu in the toolbar and click the
     pin next to "Edit in Infusion".
  2. Click its button. The test build already has access to the mock's address,
     so no permission prompt appears. That also means you won't see the
     access-request screen as a real user would; screenshot that from a normal
     install if you want it.
  3. Edit as you like. Commit is safe here: it goes to the mock's scratch copy,
     which rebuilds the site after a few seconds. The page then drops its
     "committed" frame and reloads.
  4. Close the browser to stop. The scratch copy is deleted.

  Suggested screenshots
  - Editing in the page: click into a paragraph, select a word so the toolbar
    shows, and make an edit so the frame turns to "uncommitted".
  - Source beside the page: unfold "Markdown source" with a block focused, so
    its lines are highlighted. Type [x](/docs/ to show link completion.
  - Framing:
    a. Click "Also edit framing" and choose "Footer".
    b. Edit the footer text.
    c. Open another page, e.g. /post/: its footer shows the edit, framed as
       uncommitted.

  Taking them
  - The mock's address is 127.0.0.1:port in the address bar. If you'd rather not
    show it, capture only the window content: open DevTools, then Ctrl+Shift+P
    → "Capture screenshot".
  - With DevTools' device toolbar set to 1280×800, that capture comes out at
    exactly the store's size.

  Against the real site instead
  Load extension/edit-in-infusion unpacked in your own Chrome (Developer mode →
  Load unpacked), save a token in the extension's options, and serve
  ../ponder/docs locally, e.g. python3 -m http.server -d ../ponder/docs. But
  reads and any commit then go to the real amb26/ponder repository, so for
  screenshots the mock is the safer choice.

● You're right, nothing should need eager here; the bug was in the lazy-loading
  change. It's fixed, and indexBeasBCBA.html at bagatelle's root, with its
  moduleOverrides.json5, now loads and renders.

  What went wrong: the page's <div fluid-layers="hortis.bbea.bcba"> boots while
  Infusion's files are still loading from your checkout. At that moment the
  <fluid-import> for hortis.beaVizLoader hasn't been registered yet, so the
  layer is demanded before Infusion knows where its file is. When the import is
  registered a moment later, my lazy-loading change only loads files at the
  moment of demand, so that earlier demand was lost and the file was never
  fetched. Before lazy loading, registering an import always loaded it, which is
  why ordering never mattered. The built page in docs/ wasn't affected, because
  its scripts are already inlined, so that combination only fails from the
  source page.

  Fix (fluid.loadImportMap in Fluid.js): when an import is registered for a
  layer that has already been demanded and is still undefined, its file is
  loaded and its scripts and styles are added to the document that declared the
  import.

  Error message: it said "the file imported for it was loaded but did not define
  it" when the file had never been requested. It now says "the file imported
  for it was never loaded" in that case.

  Checked:
  - In headless Chromium:
    - bagatelle's root indexBeasBCBA.html: the layer is defined, the
      visualisation renders 922 elements, and nothing is unavailable.
    - Its built docs/ version and the root indexBeasOBA.html also work.
  - npm test: 2444/2444 passed, including a new test that demands a layer, then
    declares its import, and checks the file loads.
  - Browser QUnit 397/397, and demos 34/34.

  The two moduleOverrides.json5 404s in your console are expected. The boot
  looks for the file beside docs/vendor/ and docs/ before finding it at
  bagatelle's root.

● With the clean page it passes. Now the decisive check, without the fix:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Both tests fail without the fix and pass with it, and the fix is restored.
  Full suites:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● I've added a page-level regression test, and checked it properly: with the fix
  temporarily switched off it fails, and with the fix in place it passes. The
  full suites pass: npm test 2444/2444 and browser QUnit 398/398.

  Writing it showed my earlier diagnosis was wrong about the trigger. It isn't
  dev mode or moduleOverrides.json5. It's the modules="fluid-modules.json"
  attribute on bagatelle's <fluid-module>. When a module declares a module map,
  Infusion fetches the map before it reads the page's <fluid-import>s, so the
  imports can refer to modules the map locates. That fetch is asynchronous, and
  meanwhile the page's elements boot straight away. So the element always
  demands hortis.beaVizLoader before its import exists, on every load. The built
  docs/ page escaped only because its layer's scripts are already inlined. The
  fix itself is unchanged and still correct: an import registered for a layer
  that has already been demanded is loaded at once.

  The test is a small page in tests/framework-tests/core/testData/early-demand/
  with the same shape as bagatelle's:
  - FluidBoot.js;
  - a <fluid-module> with a module map (fluid-modules.json, empty);
  - a <fluid-import> of fluid-tests-earlyDemand.vue;
  - an inline layer deriving from the imported one;
  - an element in the body booting that inline layer.

  "A page's layer deriving from one it imports renders, though its element boots
  before the import is read" in FluidViewSFCTests.js loads it in an iframe. It
  checks that the derived layer renders and that no layer is left undefined.
  Like the other iframe tests, it only runs in a real browser (npm run 
  test:browser-qunit); under node it is skipped.

  Without the fix, both this test and the narrower one from the last round
  (which declares an import after a demand) fail. The page test is the one that
  captures the real-world cause.

    fluid.markdownBlock. The generic half of ai-protocol.js is fluid-ai.js,
    under a new fluid.ai namespace. It covers the IFM, co-op and local services,
    calling them, token and energy estimates, and the conversation loop.
  - Self-contained: the panel's SFC brings everything it needs, so a host only
    imports it and offers a container. A new test page,
    components/html/AskAnythingTests.html, loads the panel with nothing of
    tldraw and checks that.
  - How a host plugs in: the panel's assistant option takes an object, or the
    global name of one, that supplies the system prompt and interprets each
    reply. With none, the panel is a plain chat.
  - What tldraw keeps: demo/tldraw/js/ai-protocol.js now holds only what's about
    the canvas: the workspace encoding, the prompts, applying changes and
    diagnosis. It hands the panel fluid.tldraw.ai.makeAssistant(bridge) through
    a small derived layer, fluid.tldraw.askAnything.

    remembered token and model choice survive the move.

  clean. Both regressions came from my lazy-import change, and both are fixed

  bagatelle's hydration round trip on indexBeasWaBA.html now passes. I ran it

  nothing was written into bagatelle. Please re-run npm run build there. It
  should copy the new bundle into docs/vendor/infusion-6 and pass.

  1. The map and network never rendered. In a hydrated page, the markup already
  holds each SFC's script, which defines its layer as the page loads. The
  template, though, is still read only from the .vue file. Under lazy loading
  the layer counts as defined, so nothing ever asked for that file, and the
  network and map waited forever for templates. Now a component waiting for a
  template triggers the load of its SFC (fluid.fetchParsedTemplate). That
  includes SFCs like hortis-bipartite.vue, whose import only becomes known once
  their parent SFC has been read (fluid.loadImportMap).

  2. Shared scripts ran twice. Several of bagatelle's SFCs share libraries, such
  as imerss-core.js, tooltip.js and Popper. When the visualisation's SFC reused
  those scripts from the markup, no record was kept that the script was already
  taken. So the checklist, network and others, loaded afterwards, injected
  their own second copies. That made the hydrated page differ from the
  dehydrated one. Reusing a script from the markup now records it as taken
  (fluid.adoptMarkupInjections / fluid.claimAdoptedScript), so other SFCs wait
  for it instead of injecting it again.

  New tests in FluidViewSFCTests.js, each confirmed to fail without its fix:
  - A page in the hydrated shape (testData/hydrated-template/), whose markup
    holds the SFC's script in the patched form the build writes, renders from
    the SFC's template.
  - A script reused from the markup by one SFC isn't injected again for another.

  first problem was missed earlier because my test runs used the stale bundle
  rather than the source.

● No, it wasn't always the case, and I worded that badly. Both problems trace
  back to one change of mine: making <fluid-import> lazy. I made it when you
  asked that pages load only the SFCs they reference.

  What changed. In the committed code (6.3.0), fluid.loadImportMap fetched every
  imported SFC as soon as its import was read. A comment there even said that
  demand-driven loading was planned for the future. fluid.fetchParsedTemplate
  never triggered a load, because it never needed to: by the time a template was
  wanted, its SFC was already loading. My lazy change made the load start only
  when a layer is demanded. In a hydrated page the layer is already defined by
  the markup, so it's never demanded, and nothing fetched the SFC for its
  template. The template trigger I added today restores what eager loading used
  to provide.

  The shared scripts running twice come from a gap that was already there, and
  that my change exposed:
  - fluid.adoptMarkupInjections reuses a script from the hydrated markup but
    doesn't record a shared-script claim. That's unchanged since 6.3.0.
  - fluid.markupScriptFrom deliberately skips markup scripts that have already
    been adopted. Also unchanged.
  - So once the visualisation's SFC has adopted, say, imerss-core.js, an SFC
    handled after it finds neither a claim nor an unadopted markup copy, and
    injects the script again.

  Under eager loading every SFC loaded at boot, and this evidently didn't
  happen, since 6.3.0 passes the round trip. My guess is that the nested SFCs
  were handled before the parent adopted the shared scripts. They then found the
  markup copies still unadopted and treated them as already run. Lazy loading
  reverses that order, because the parent's SFC is now fetched first, for its
  own template, and the nested ones only afterwards. I haven't confirmed that
  ordering by running 6.3.0, though; it's an inference.

  So today's adoption fix closes a gap that was already in the committed code
  and relied on load order to stay hidden.

  Earlier symptoms of the same change, all from this lazy-import work:
  - The tldraw layer picker needed the new eager attribute.
  - bagatelle's source page needed loads to start for layers demanded before
    their import was read.
  - The "Ask me anything" panel's hidden-element rule, which lived in the entry
    SFC, no longer applied once that SFC loaded later.

  Lazy loading changes when and in what order SFCs arrive, and several places
  had relied on everything arriving together at boot.

  Factoring of "Ask me anything"

  - What's bundled with the panel: a new core file,
    src/components/askAnything/fluid-ai-arena.js (fluid.ai.arena). The panel's
    SFC loads it alongside fluid-ai.js. It holds:
    - encoding the workspace as PTF;
    - parsing, planning, checking and stamping the AI's changes;
    - diagnosing widgets;
    - the assistant;
    - the steps every bridge shares.
  - What's left in tldraw: only what is genuinely tldraw's. That's the shape and
    canvas parts, planning shape parts, geometry, and creating shapes through
    the editor. tldraw passes these to the core protocol as an arena "host"; its
    existing functions remain as thin wrappers over the core.
  - The common parent: both arenas are widgets that are children of one root
    (fluid.history.arenaRoot). So the core can find widgets as the root's
    children. fluid.ai.arena.makeBridge is the bridge for an arena with no host
    of its own, such as a page edited in place: it creates and destroys children
    of the root. tldraw's bridge reuses the shared steps for registering
    layers, applying changes to a widget in place, and diagnosing before and
    after.
  - System prompt as a component: fluid.ai.arena.systemPrompt holds stanzas,
    each {order, text} by name. A derived layer merges in stanzas or replaces
    them. fluid.tldraw.ai.systemPrompt replaces the introduction, and adds
    canvas placement rules (order 35) and an editor hint (order 45).
  - Generic text: the core's own stanzas no longer mention canvases or shapes,
    and its worked examples have no shape parts.
  - Tests: new ones in AskAnythingTests drive a plain arena with no tldraw code
    loaded. They check:
    - a derived layer's stanza lands in its order;
    - the workspace description is free of host material;
    - a widget is changed in place, created and deleted.
  - A latent bug, now fixed: my previous refactor left error-reporting paths in
    three tldraw files calling fluid.tldraw.ai.describeError and listProblems,
    which no longer existed. Those paths would have thrown, and no test
    exercised them.

  fluid.tldraw.hostPotentiaFor

  What it's for: the host has to give a widget its container, shape id and shape
  configuration, which belong on whichever view actually renders. When a
  widget's view is borrowed from a subcomponent (view: "{first}.view"), that
  view lives inside first. Settings aimed at the widget's own view would
  override the borrowing. So the function works out where the effective view
  lives.

  Why it's fragile:
  - It matches the view reference against two regexes, so it fails for any other
    form: a deeper path, a computed view, or a reference through another
    context name.
  - It reads the internal contributions of the merged definition, and recurses
    by guessing the member's layer as the last one listed.
  - In effect it re-implements reference resolution outside the framework, and
    in a "push" style.

  More stable alternative: let the view pull, instead of the host pushing.
  1. The host supplies one record at the widget's root, which always exists:
     e.g. hosting: {container, shapeId, shape}, as potentia at "/".
  2. fluid.topLevelWidget gives each nested top-level widget a default hosting
     taken from the enclosing one. That's the same pattern it already uses for
     enclosingHostBounds via bindEnclosingHostBounds.
  3. fluid.tldrawViewComponent, which the driver already applies to every
     top-level widget's view, reads container, shapeId and shape from its own
     component's hosting.

  A borrowed view ({first}.view) then finds the umbrella's record through first,
  whatever form the reference takes. No regexes, no merge internals. It would
  also simplify persistence: writeShapeConfig would only edit one root-level
  member instead of finding a view path.

  I haven't implemented this. It changes how every widget is hosted and how
  shapes persist, so it's worth agreeing the shape of hosting first.

  Not yet done

  fluid.ai.arena.makeBridge is ready for a page edited in place, but the
  extension's panel doesn't offer "Ask me anything" yet. That's the next
  integration step. The new structure is written up in section 3.11 of the
  working doc.

❯ The hosting notion sounds good. What layers pull shapeId and shape?           

● Let me check what actually reads them, rather than answer from memory:

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● Only one layer pulls either of them, and only shapeId is actually used. shape
  is never read by any layer.

  shapeId is read by fluid.tldrawViewComponent in tldraw-driver.js, and only for
  one thing. Its hostBounds binding,
  fluid.tldraw.bindShapeBounds({self}.editor, {self}.shapeId), tracks the bounds
  of the widget's shape through the editor. From there it reaches widgets only
  indirectly: fluid.topLevelWidget reads view.hostBounds to compute its own
  hostBounds (falling back to the enclosing widget's), which is what widgets and
  the AI's prompt use. A nested widget gets no shapeId (it defaults to null),
  so it reports no bounds and takes the enclosing widget's. That's the case
  hostPotentiaFor routes around for borrowed views.

  shape is declared by fluid.tldrawViewComponent with defaults (x, y, w, h,
  rotation, isLocked, opacity, parentId, index), but nothing reads it
  reactively. It's a passenger, there so the shape's configuration travels
  inside the widget's PTF:
  - The host supplies it at construction (InfusionHost, via hostPotentiaFor).
  - When a widget is copied or persisted, the live configuration comes from the
    editor (fluid.tldraw.shapeToConfig), not from this member.
  - fluid.tldraw.writeShapeConfig then rewrites or strips it in the parts.
  - It reads the defaults from the layer's definition
    (readLayerDef("fluid.tldrawViewComponent").shape), so that default values
    aren't transmitted.

  What that means for the hosting record:
  - container is consumed by the view's rendering, so the view must pull it.
  - shapeId is needed only where hostBounds is bound, so that binding pulls it.
  - shape doesn't need to be on the view at all. It can sit inert at the
    widget's root as hosting.shape. Then writeShapeConfig only edits that one
    root-level member, instead of locating a view potentia path, which today
    means following the same borrowed-view routing.

  So in practice the hosting change only needs to move two consumers.
  fluid.tldrawViewComponent would read container and shapeId from its own
  component's hosting, and writeShapeConfig would work on the root. The shape
  defaults would move with it, to wherever hosting is declared.

❯ Why couldn't the host simply supply "container" as a standard argument        
  targetted at view.container as one would know any viewComponent at the root   
  would expect?                                                                 

● The relevant facts are in Infusion's merge rules and its container forwarding,
  so let me check both:

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● It can, and for most widgets that's exactly what happens. hostPotentiaFor
  falls through to {view: {$component: {container, shapeId, shape}}} whenever
  the widget's view is its own. Infusion even does this for you with a free
  component: fluid.upgradeFreeComponentArgs forwards a top-level container
  argument to view.$component.container. The convention breaks in one case only:
  a widget whose view is borrowed from a subcomponent.

  Why the borrowed view breaks it. An umbrella widget can say view: 
  "{first}.view", where the root's view member is a reference, not a $component
  record. Potentia are just the strongest layer, and the merge rules say a
  stronger non-object value replaces a weaker one wholesale, and vice versa. So
  host potentia of view: {$component: {container}} doesn't add a container to
  the borrowed view. It replaces the reference with a fresh, empty view
  component at the umbrella's root:
  - That component has no layers or template, so it renders nothing into the
    container.
  - first's view, which holds the template, never receives the container, so
    nothing renders at all.

  hostPotentiaFor exists to dodge this: it steers the potentia to first.view,
  where the view really lives.

  Why the free-component courtesy doesn't apply. tldraw's widgets are
  constructed as children of tldrawHost (fluid.initChildComponent), not as free
  components. And forwarding would hit the same problem anyway, since it writes
  the same view.$component record.

  So the standard argument is fine as long as the root's view is a component
  record, which is the assumption "any viewComponent at the root" makes. The
  trouble is that Infusion lets the root's view be a reference into the widget's
  own tree, and the AI's composition advice in the prompt encourages exactly
  that.

  There are two ways to keep the standard argument and still cover that case:

  1. Pull, not push (the hosting idea). The host writes only to the root, which
     always exists. Whichever view ends up rendering reads its container upward
     through its component's hosting, however it was reached. The view then has
     no need to be at the root at all.
  2. A merge rule letting potentia refine a reference. A $component record
     merged over a reference to a component would mean "apply these options to
     the referenced component" rather than replacing it. Then view: {$component:
     {container}} would land on first.view, and the standard argument would
     just work. That's a change to Infusion's merge semantics, with wider
     consequences. It means writing into a component owned elsewhere in the
     tree, which could be another widget entirely if the reference leaves the
     widget. So I'd treat it as a design question rather than a quick fix.

  I'd still go with the first.

● I've sketched it, and it fits the existing code closely; no code is changed
  yet. The sketch is in a-scratch/reports/injected-site-refinement.md.

  The rule. A $component record that names no $layers, landing on a member that
  holds a reference, refines the component the reference injects, instead of
  replacing the reference. A record that does name $layers still constructs a
  fresh component and replaces it, as now. Plain subcomponents already work this
  way: a layerless $component record accumulates onto the subcomponent that
  weaker records define. So the host's view: {$component: {container}} would
  mean the same whether the view is built at the site or borrowed. The standard
  argument, including Infusion's own container forwarding for free components,
  would just work.

  How it would be built:
  1. Merge (fluid.collectComponentRecords, Fluid.js:2550). Today a stronger
     record wipes the reference (reference = undefined). Instead, a layerless
     record after a reference would be kept as a refinement, passed alongside
     the reference in the layer map. There's a precedent: a reference's fallback
     (the weaker material it overrides) already travels that way. Merging can't
     know whether a reference designates a component, so it decides only by the
     record's shape. The effect waits until the reference resolves.
  2. Injection (fluid.expandReferenceRecord). A reference to a component already
     has an injector effect that registers the target at the site and withdraws
     it later. Registering would also hand the refinements to the target, and
     withdrawing (on retarget or destroy) would take them back.
  3. The target's merge (FluidIL.js:3440). Each component's merge would also
     take the refinements handed to it. They'd use the distribution merge-record
     type, which is defined but unused. Its priority puts it above the target's
     own definition, its parent's records and its own constructor arguments,
     but below template entries, dynamic layers and live writes. That's where
     Infusion 4 placed distributions. The target remerges as refinements come
     and go.
  4. The subtle part: scope. A reference written inside a refinement, such as
     {umbrella}.selection, must resolve as it would at the injecting site, not
     at the target. So such references get rewritten as global references from
     the injecting site before the refinements are handed over. $for already
     does this for valueAs. {self} still means the target, as in any $component
     record.

  Decisions needed before building:
  - Reach. The target is one component, so a refinement through one site is seen
    at every site. Should a site only be able to refine a target inside its own
    tree, as Infusion 4 allowed distributions only downward? Or any target,
    since a reference can point sideways or upward?
  - Conflicts. Is ordering competing refinements by path enough, or should a
    refinement carry a priority, as distributions did?
  - $layers in a refinement. I've excluded them to keep the refine/replace rule
    purely about the record's shape. Distributing layers could come later
    through an explicit marker such as $refine: true.

  With this in place, hostPotentiaFor and its regexes collapse to the standard
  view argument for every widget, writeShapeConfig edits one fixed path, and no
  special {hosting} context is needed. The sketch ends with seven tests for
  FluidILTests. I'd build it once you've settled the reach question, which
  affects the safety checks more than the mechanics.

      12  the facility intended for Infusion 4's distributions. Motivated

● Refinement through injected sites is built: options with no $layers at an
  injected site now merge into the component injected there, with any reach,
  ordered by path. All suites pass: Infusion 2523/2523, browser QUnit 411/411,
  demos 34/34.

  How it works:
  - Merge (fluid.collectComponentRecords, Fluid.js). A $component record with no
    $layers, stronger than a reference, no longer wipes the reference. It's
    kept as a refinement and carried beside the reference in the layer map, the
    same way a reference's fallback is. The member's merged value stays a plain
    reference string, so nothing else that reads merged members is affected. A
    record that names $layers still constructs a fresh component and replaces
    the reference.
  - Injection (FluidIL.js). A member reference with refinements is expanded
    through a new record type, compared by content. A change in the refinements
    therefore re-expands the injection, rather than silently reusing it.
    - Registering the target hands the refinements over
      (fluid.distributeRefinements); withdrawal, retargeting or destruction
      takes them back (fluid.retractRefinements).
    - References written inside a refinement are rewritten as global references
      from the injecting site (fluid.globaliseRefinement), so {umbrella}.note
      means the injecting umbrella even at a target far away. {self} still means
      the target.
    - If a refined reference resolves to something that isn't a component, the
      member is unavailable, with a message suggesting $layers.
  - The target's merge. Each component now holds the refinements handed to it,
    keyed by injecting path, and merges them under the reserved, previously
    unused distribution type. That puts them above its own definition and
    constructor options, but below template entries, dynamic layers and live
    writes. Several sites are ordered by path, the later winning. The layer map
    names each source, e.g. distribution from umbrella-12.view (user).

  Tests (FluidILTests): five new tests, four of which fail with the feature
  disabled. The fifth checks that $layers still replaces the reference, so it
  correctly passes either way. They cover:
  - options reaching a borrowed view;
  - $layers still constructing a fresh component;
  - references resolving where they were written, and retraction when the
    injecting site is destroyed;
  - ordering by path, and the priority against the target's own options and live
    writes;
  - the not-a-component case.

  tldraw. hostPotentiaFor is now one line, {view: {$component: {container, 
  shapeId, shape}}}; the regexes and the reading of merge internals are gone. An
  umbrella whose view is borrowed renders through it purely by refinement. The
  existing test of that rendering passes, and only the two tests asserting the
  old potentia shape needed new expectations. writeShapeConfig writes the shape
  at that one path. It also moves any configuration persisted the old way, at
  the subcomponent lending the view, which a new assertion covers.

  Still to do: the PTF round-trip test from the sketch, and documenting the rule
  in fluid-integration-language.md. The sketch file now records what was built.

  documentation's example caught nothing wrong in the feature, but did turn up
  one cosmetic fix. Everything passes: Infusion 2533/2533, browser QUnit
  413/413, demos 34/34.

  PTF round trip (FluidPTFTests.js, "Options refining a borrowed view
  transmitted and reconstructed"). It builds an umbrella that borrows its
  subcomponent's view, created with view: {$component: {colour: "blue"}}, and
  also writes size live through the borrowed view. It then checks:
  - the refinement is transmitted where it was written, in the umbrella's root
    potentia, and nothing of it lands in the parts of the view it refines;
  - after destroying the umbrella and deleting both layer definitions,
    reconstructing from the PTF text alone gives an umbrella still borrowing the
    view, refined blue again and holding the live size.

  It passes, and fails with refinement disabled.

  Documentation (ponder's content/docs/fluid-integration-language.md):
  - Merging and precedence: a distribution row in the table, and a merge-rules
    bullet stating the rule (no $layers refines, $layers replaces).
  - $component: "must name $layers" now gives its two exceptions, accumulating
    onto a weaker record and refining an injected component.
  - Injecting an existing component: the claim that a record can always override
    a reference now says this needs $layers.
  - New subsection, Refining an injected component: the principle, with a
    borrowed-view example where a creator's container argument refines the view.
    It also covers:
    - where a refinement stands among the merge types;
    - the target being one component at every site, of any reach;
    - ordering by path;
    - references resolving where they were written, with {self} meaning the
      target;
    - withdrawal, plain-data targets, and PTF transmission.

  record name ending in empty parentheses, because those arguments have no
  record name. The name now reads distribution from <path> in that case.

● The list scenario passes 19/19. Rerunning the other two scenarios and lint
  after the bridge change.

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● All of it is built except images, which I've sketched rather than built. All
  three extension scenarios pass: the new list scenario 19/19, framing 23/23 and
  block editor 32/32. Lint is clean. I haven't looked at the startup on screen:
  the jank fixes rest on the causes I found in the code, and the tests only
  show that the behaviour still works.

  "Edit as source" is now a disclosure with the rotating chevron from
  bagatelle's filter panels. Your fold choice is remembered across every panel
  on every site. It goes in the extension's own chrome.storage.local, not
  IndexedDB. That's the idiomatic place for extension settings: any part of the
  extension can read it at startup, and it keeps settings apart from claims,
  which are the data being edited. If you'd like the choice to follow you across
  machines, swapping in chrome.storage.sync is a one-line change. The source is
  still forced open when nothing else can edit the target: framing, a new post,
  or blocks that can't be edited in place. That forced opening isn't
  remembered.

  /post opening the footer: a page with no source of its own used to default to
  the first framing source, which is the footer. It now edits nothing until you
  choose something, and the panel says what you can do.

  New post: with the editor open, a "+" sits at the head of the list.
  - It asks for a title and builds front matter with the title and today's date.
  - The file path follows the title until commit, e.g.
    content/post/2026-11-21-a-post-written-in-place.md, avoiding any path the
    site already has.
  - Commit creates the file. New posts not yet published appear at the head of
    the list, marked by state; clicking one resumes editing it.
  - For this, ponder's trace.js now adds a section record to list pages'
    linkage. Pages built before that work out the section from their path.
    ponder's docs/ build hasn't been regenerated.

  Editor staying open across navigation: whether the panel is open, and whether
  framing is being edited, is kept per tab in sessionStorage. The editor reopens
  on the next page and closing it forgets it. This only works on sites you've
  granted access to. Testing it turned up a real bug: reopening at page load can
  race a page that boots its own Infusion for a live island, and that boot
  removed the panel. The panel and resize bar are now put back if detached,
  except while the bridge has deliberately withdrawn them during its own boot.

  Startup jank: I removed the causes I found.
  - The panel used to appear and then vanish while Infusion booted. The page is
    now made live first and the panel is shown once, with a short fade-in.
  - The panel's width flipped when the source folded after boot. The remembered
    fold state now applies before the panel shows.
  - Docking reset the page to the top. The scroll position is now carried
    across.
  - Bootstrap's label styles were leaking into the panel; they're now
    overridden.

  Framing: "Also edit framing" is a tick-box. Ticking it marks each framing
  element as editable, and clicking one (the footer, say) loads its source, with
  the edit rendered live in place. A first click selects the element rather
  than following its links; once it's being edited, clicks pass through as
  normal. Clicking a block of the page's own content goes back to the page's
  source. The drop-down is gone. Site configuration (wend.json) has no element
  of its own, so it gets a small button that appears in framing mode.

  Images: the sketch is in a-scratch/reports/images-in-place.md. The main change
  it needs is that a claim becomes a changeset across several files, committed
  through the Git Data API, because an image adds a binary file and rename and
  delete touch many files at once.
  - Images go to static/img/<post-slug>-<n>.<ext>.
  - They show at once from blob: URLs until published.
  - Rename and delete need ponder's trace to record, for each source, which
    assets it references. Delete warns if other pages still link the image.

  Code changes:
  - the extension's edit.js, bridge.js, background.js and edit.css;
  - the test harness, the framing scenario, and the new
    extension/test/list-scenario.js;
  - ponder's infusion/js/trace.js.

● I've built and tested step 1 of the images plan. Widget insertion, widget
  paste and the wend / beautiful-wend / ponder split are designed but not yet
  built. All five extension scenarios pass: changeset 14/14, list 19/19, framing
  23/23, block editor 32/32. Lint is clean. After those runs I only changed
  comments and lint annotations.

  Step 1: claims of several files, committed as one

  - Claims can now hold further files beside their main source, in Claim.files.
    Each entry has its content as base64 (or null to remove the file), the blob
    sha it replaces, and a hash.
  - Committing: a claim with further files goes through the Git Data API as one
    commit (fluidGitHub.commitChangeset in github.js). There are two checks:
    - Each file is checked against the branch head before anything is written. A
      conflict names the files that changed, and the claim keeps that list in
      conflicts.
    - The branch only moves if no one else has committed meanwhile.

    A claim of one file still goes through the Contents API as before.
  - Knowing when it's published: ponder's trace now records a hash for every
    static file (staticFiles). A claim is dropped only once its main source and
    every further file are published, or removed where that was the edit.
  - Mock GitHub gains the Git Data endpoints (refs, commits, trees, blobs) and
    refuses a branch move that isn't a fast-forward.
  - The new scenario (extension/test/changeset-scenario.js):
    - commits a post together with a new image in static/img, and checks that
      both are published and the claim is then dropped;
    - commits nothing when an image being removed was changed by someone else
      meanwhile, and names that image;
    - commits a rename (remove one image, add the other) as one commit once the
      claim is read afresh.

  Widgets and the split: design only

  The design is in a-scratch/reports/widgets-in-content.md.

  How a widget is written in markdown: the island element we already use
  (fluid-layers), plus fluid-id so it keeps its identity across re-renders. Its
  potentia (settings and state) goes in a child <script 
  type="application/fluid-potentia+json">. The toolbar's "+", copy, paste and
  saving state back into the markdown all use one encoder/decoder, which belongs
  in Infusion core beside the PTF code. Pasted PTF puts every layer except the
  widget's own into static/sfc as further files of the claim. Anything in
  static/sfc that reaches fluid.topLevelWidget appears on the toolbar.

  You were right that there are holes. These are the main ones:
  1. An island receives only flat string data- attributes. Self-booting elements
     receive not even those.
  2. Neither has anywhere to keep nested components' settings or live state,
     both of which PTF carries.
  3. Nothing writes an island's live state back into the markdown, so an edited
     widget is lost on save.
  4. bootLayers in linkage.json is kept by hand, so a newly added widget would
     silently fail to boot.
  5. fillIslands matches islands by their attributes alone, so two counters with
     different settings would be swapped.

  The report also covers layers written as JavaScript rather than SFCs, and
  functions that can't travel. The fixes for the first two holes need changes in
  Infusion's island and self-boot code.

  The split:
  - wend: the build, markdown pipeline, trace, linkage, page boot, content and
    island layers, and the editing contracts.
  - beautiful-wend: the header, navbar and footer, previews, pagers, tags,
    comments, i18n and theme CSS.
  - ponder: content, wend.json, linkage.json, its own shortcodes and widgets,
    and its static files.

  Three choices in it are yours:
  - Renaming layers: ponder.* → wend.* / beautifulWend.*, keeping aliases for a
    release so saved content still resolves.
  - Packaging: npm packages, or checkouts resolved through the module map.
  - Editing a theme's framing: I propose that it creates a site-level override
    in the site's own files rather than editing the theme. That is the same rule
    as pasting.

  buildSite.js is the place to cut first, since it mixes the generic build with
  ponder's own paths.

  The next step I'd suggest is the first item in the report's order of work: the
  potentia script on islands, fixing the first two holes and the matching one,
  with tests in FluidViewTests.

  Besides the new scenario, the code changes are in the extension's github.js,
  background.js, claims.js and edit.js, in extension/test/mock-github.js, and in
  ponder's trace.js and buildSite.js. ponder's published docs/ has not been
  rebuilt, so the live site's trace lacks staticFiles until it is.

  Lint is clean in both repositories. In one combined run, one block-editor
  check ("The cursor in the source marks its block in the page") failed. It
  passed when rerun alone, so it looks like a timing flake under load. Nothing
  is committed.

  One change from the design: a widget's settings now live in an attribute,
  fluid-potentia='{…}', not a child <script>. Building it showed that an
  island's own render replaces its element's children but keeps its attributes.
  A script would therefore vanish from statically built pages and on every
  re-render. Live state goes at $live in the same JSON, keyed by component path
  as PTF's live parts are, and is applied when the island is first created.

  1. Core (Infusion): islands and self-booting elements now both read
     fluid-potentia. Before, an island got only its data- attributes and a
     self-booting element got nothing. Nested components and live state are
     carried too. Island matching in edit.fillIslands now includes fluid-id and
     fluid-potentia, so two differently configured counters aren't swapped. New
     tests are in FluidViewTests.
  2. ponder's build:
     - It imports static/sfc/*.vue, both under node and in published pages.
     - Every such layer is treated as needing boot, so a new widget no longer
       silently fails to load.
     - The linkage lists the widgets that reach fluid.topLevelWidget.
  3. Converting to and from PTF, in FluidPTF.js: a set of fluid.ptf.island*
     functions. Leaving a widget writes its state back into the markdown, and
     reloading restores it. Tested in FluidPTFTests.
  4. Toolbar: a widget menu plus "+" in the block editor.
  5. Copy and paste:
     - Copying a widget puts PTF and its markup on the clipboard. Pasting PTF,
       into a block or the source view, inserts the widget and renders it at
       once.
     - Its layers become further files of the claim in static/sfc. A layer the
       site already holds identically is skipped; one it holds differently is
       replaced only if you confirm.
     - The new widget scenario covers the whole cycle: inserting a counter,
       clicking it, pasting a new widget, committing both files in one commit,
       publishing, and the count surviving a reload.
  6. The split (in ponder):
     - packages/wend: the build, model, markdown pipeline, trace and page boot,
       plus the content, tag and alias SFCs.
     - packages/beautiful-wend: the theme's SFCs, its adaptations, and its
       static files moved from themes/beautifulhugo/static.
     - ponder itself: content, configuration, the host document and its
       shortcodes, plus a new wend.site.json describing the layout.
     - Verification: I built before and after the move, and every page renders
       identically apart from module declarations and hashed paths.
     - Fork-on-write: the first edit of the footer creates
       infusion/override/beautifulWend/sfc/ponder-footer.vue, read from the
       theme's published copy, and the theme's file stays untouched. The build
       then uses the fork in place of the theme's file. The framing scenario
       checks this through to the published site.

  - I didn't set up npm workspaces, because that would change ponder's lockfile

● The split moved the code into the new packages, but every layer still has a
  name from before it. That makes the names wrong in two ways:

  - The prefix names the site, not the package. ponder.document, ponder.content,
    ponder.scriptTag and ponder.stylesheetTag now live in packages/wend.
    ponder.header, ponder.navbar, ponder.footer, ponder.main.*,
    ponder.postMeta.* and the rest (about 60 layers) live in
    packages/beautiful-wend. A second site built on these packages would get
    layers named after ponder.
  - The filenames follow the old names. The build works out a layer's name from
    its file (ponder-footer.vue → ponder.footer). Renaming the layers therefore
    means renaming the files too.

  What the rename would do

  1. Give each package its own namespace:
     - wend's layers become wend.document, wend.content, wend.scriptTag and so
       on.
     - The theme's layers become beautifulWend.header, beautifulWend.footer,
       beautifulWend.main.list and so on. My earlier note said "wend.*" loosely;
       I'd suggest the theme gets a prefix of its own, matching its module name
       in wend.site.json.
     - The theme's adaptations (adapt/gcse, adapt/staticman, …) follow the same
       pattern, e.g. beautifulWend.navbar.gcse.
  2. Leave ponder's own layers alone. The shortcodes (ponder.shortcode.figure,
     ponder.shortcode.vizreactive, …) and anything else under infusion/ really
     do belong to ponder, so ponder.* is right for them.
  3. Rename the files to match, e.g.
     packages/beautiful-wend/sfc/ponder-footer.vue → beautifulWend-footer.vue.
     Every $layers reference, every fluid.def, and the name lists in
     siteModel.js, markdown.js and trace.js would change with them.
  4. Keep the old names as aliases. wend already has an alias SFC for this. Each
     old name would be defined as a thin layer over its new one, roughly
     fluid.def("ponder.footer", {$layers: "beautifulWend.footer"}), or listed in
     one alias table. That keeps these working:
     - Content: markdown that names a layer directly, for example an island with
       fluid-layers="ponder.…".
     - The linkage: infusion/linkage.json's framing entries, which name layers
       such as ponder.footer.
     - Forks: an existing override like
       infusion/override/beautifulWend/sfc/ponder-footer.vue. Its path and the
       layer it defines would both need mapping to the new name.
     - Published pages: the published trace and linkage, and any uncommitted
       claims in the extension, still refer to the old names until the site is
       rebuilt.
     - The extension's tests, which name ponder.footer, ponder.main.list and
       others.
  5. Check it the same way as the split. Build before and after, and every page
     should render the same apart from layer names in the module declarations
     and linkage. Then rerun the extension's five scenarios, which cover
     framing, forks and widgets.

  Why I left it

  The split was a pure file move, and I checked it by comparing the built pages.
  Renaming at the same time would have made that comparison much harder to
  read. The rename also touches nearly every SFC and every naming list, so it's
  best done as a separate step. The one decision that's yours is the theme's
  prefix: beautifulWend.* (my suggestion) or a shared wend.*.

● The rename is done and all suites pass. There are no aliases, as you said, and
  nothing is committed or pushed.

  What changed (ponder):
  - Layer names: wend's 4 layers are now wend.* (e.g. wend.content) and the
    theme's ~60 are beautifulWend.*. Their function namespaces moved with them
    (beautifulWend.site.lookupPages, beautifulWend.urlize, …). ponder's own
    shortcodes stay ponder.shortcode.*.
  - Files: 61 renamed to match, e.g. sfc/beautifulWend-footer.vue. I updated
    every reference in infusion/site.html, infusion/linkage.json, wend.json
    (commentsLayer), the READMEs and the extension's test.
  - wend no longer names its theme's root layer: wend.site.json gains "root": 
    "beautifulWend.site". The build reads it, and each page's linkage carries it
    to the browser as migration.root (the extension's edit.js and bridge.js
    pass it on).
  - Stale forks: the build now reports and ignores a fork in infusion/override
    that matches no module file, e.g. one under a renamed file's old name.
    Before, it would have quietly stood in for nothing.
  - I left the historical REQUIREMENTS*.md and transcripts with the old names.

  Infusion core bug the rename exposed. On /post the list emptied in the
  browser, with "Global value beautifulWend.site.lookupPages is not defined".
  - Cause: the page declares <fluid-module id="beautifulWend">. In a browser, an
    element's id is also reachable as a global of that name, so
    window.beautifulWend was that element. Infusion wrote the layers' namespaces
    onto the element, and they were lost. The old ponder.* names never matched
    a module id, so this never showed.
  - Fix: fluid.getGlobalValue and setGlobalValue in Fluid.js now only treat a
    path as rooted at a property the window really holds, via a new
    fluid.isOwnGlobal. A new test in FluidViewTests covers it.
  - This would bite any site whose module id matches its layer prefix, which is
    now the convention.

      1 // The runes of Infusion 6's configuration - the interior of a St
        ring written in a layer record, as Infusion reads it.
      2 // This grammar is nested by src/fluidLint.js within @lezer/javas
        cript, over the interior of each String, and each
      3 // template literal, which configures a layer - see docs/fluid-in
        tegration-language.md, "References" and "Signal
      4 // directives". It parses the text as written in source, so that
        the positions of its nodes are those of the source -
      5 // a backslash written `\\` in JavaScript is two characters here.
      6 //

● I've built the lint package and the live example widget, and migrated all 77
  code examples in the six docs pages except one. Every example lints clean and
  none produces a run error. Each page shows an editor per example, and examples
  that define a view show their instance at the left. Nothing is committed, and
  ponder's docs/ hasn't been rebuilt.

  The lint package (infusion-6/packages/fluid-lint/):
  - The grammar (grammar/fluid-runes.grammar) covers what's inside configuration
    strings: references like {self my.widget}.title or {0}:query, compact
    records like $compute:fn({self}.a, 3), backslash escapes, plain literals,
    template @{…} interpolation, and the call bodies of $lens and $bindable.
  - Mixed mode: the grammar nests inside @lezer/javascript, but only over
    strings within a fluid.def record. Strings inside function bodies are
    treated as code and left alone. In .vue files, it applies to each top-level
    <script> and to <template>.
  - The linter checks:
    - every rune down to its interior, and the compact directive names;
    - where each $ key may sit, the keys and required members of each long form
      ($compute, $effect, $method, $lens, $bindable, $linkage, $for), and
      $component records recursively.
    - Fragments such as view: {…} are linted as if inside a record.
  - Tests: 29 node tests. It runs clean over all 129 Infusion, ponder and
    extension source files bar one.
  - Bundle: npm run build regenerates the parser and bundles it with CodeMirror
    6 into src/lib/fluid-lint/fluid-lint.js (720KB minified). That's a committed
    build artefact, like the extension's CodeMirror bundle. Runes are
    highlighted in the editor.

  The widget (src/components/sfc/fluid-liveExample.vue):
  - Built pages show just the code. In the browser it loads the bundle and
    becomes a three-part widget: the editor at the right, the console below, and
    any view instance at the left.
  - Code reruns whenever it lints without errors, and the previous run's
    components are destroyed first.
  - Example code receives console and container. If the code defines a
    view-bearing layer and doesn't create it, the widget creates the last such
    layer itself.
  - Tests: 4 Chromium tests (LiveExampleTests.html) cover running, the console,
    the instance, rerunning on edit, an error stopping the run, and fragments.

  Docs migration (ponder):
  - Markdown: a fence marked js live or html live becomes the widget, and other
    renderers still see an ordinary js fence. Each docs page gets a short note
    explaining the live examples.
  - Fragments: 12 examples use variables or layers they never define (that,
    cell, my.header…), so I marked them js live fragment: linted but not run.
    They're the candidates for making self-contained.
  - Left static: the one syntax summary ({func: …} / "$compute:…") isn't code,
    so I didn't convert it.
  - Container: two examples now use the widget's {container} instead of
    document.getElementById(...).

  Bugs found and fixed along the way:
  - wend dropped imports: imports from %infusion-6/… in the host document never
    reached published pages, because the regex didn't allow the hyphen.
  - Escaping: example code starting with { or $ would have been read as a
    reference or directive, so I escape it.
  - Duplicate CodeMirror: @codemirror/lint brought its own copies of view and
    state, which silently disabled the linter. I aligned the versions.

  Test results:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬───────────┐
  │              Suite               │  Result   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │ Infusion npm test                │ 2567/2567 │

  ├──────────────────────────────────┼───────────┤

  ├──────────────────────────────────┼───────────┤
  │ Extension scenario: block editor │ 32/32     │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴───────────┘

  The block-editor scenario's known cursor-timing check failed once in the batch
  and passed when rerun alone. Lint is clean.

  Things to know:
  - Dependencies: I installed @lezer/generator, the lezer parsers, CodeMirror 6
    and esbuild from npm into packages/fluid-lint (its node_modules is
    git-ignored).
  - Layer collisions: examples on one page share global layer names, so
    rerunning one that redefines my.app also changes other live instances of
    my.app on the page.
  - Extension untested: the editing extension treats a live fence as an island,
    but I haven't tested editing one in its block editor.
  - Bug in Infusion: the linter flags a stray args outside the $method record in
    src/framework/edit/sfc/fluid-editorRoot.vue:99. I left it, since it happens
    to be harmless.

  contents are renamed, the Infusion slip is fixed, the linter tests have gone
  from 29 to 124 and all pass, and error recovery is better. Nothing is
  committed.

  Layer collisions. Only these four were redefined on the same page with
  different contents. I renamed the later example each time, along with its
  references:
  - IL page, stylesheet example: my.page → my.styledPage (and {page} →
    {styledPage}).
  - IL page, $reactiveRoot example: my.todoList → my.checklist.
  - IL page, $importMap example: my.app → my.chartApp.
  - fluid-view page, placeholder example: my.site → my.recordsSite.

  One my.app collision remains on the IL page, but the second one is a fragment
  that never runs. Layers sharing a prefix, like my.app and my.app.counter,
  don't clobber each other.

  Identical redefinition. No example pair redefines a layer with identical
  contents, but rerunning an edited example does. I checked in node that
  redefining a layer with an identical new record doesn't recompute a live
  instance's $compute, and that a real change does. I checked this for computed
  values only, not for re-rendering of a live view.

  Infusion fix. In src/framework/edit/sfc/fluid-editorRoot.vue, goToLayerRef's
  args now sits inside its $method record. Without it, the method was probably
  called without self bound, so it may have been a real bug rather than
  harmless.

  Linter tests (packages/fluid-lint/test/lintTests.js, 124 tests):
  - Correct styles: every reference form (selectors, labels, $parent, $oldValue,
    numeric segments), compact records with numbers, booleans and bare
    arguments, escapes, templates, each member directive in full form,
    $component with $for and $if, fragments and SFCs.
  - Malformations: each checks the severity, the exact text the error covers,
    and the message.
  - Code left alone: strings inside functions and outside fluid.def aren't
    linted.
  - Several faults at once: texts with four to six faults each, checked to
    report every one without a cascade of errors.

  Error recovery and messages:
  - Missing commas: before, one missing comma between members turned every later
    line into "Syntax error" and hid the rune checks. Now it's reported as
    expected "," between the members of an object and repaired in place without
    moving any positions, so linting carries on past it.
  - Brackets: a mismatched or unclosed bracket names the line of the bracket
    left open, e.g. expected "}" to close the "{" on line 1. Line numbers are
    correct within fragments and SFCs.
  - Inside strings: the four generic "Malformed …" messages are replaced by
    specific ones: unclosed reference or call, empty context or argument,
    missing path segment, label or :, a missing comma between arguments, text
    after a complete reference or compact record, and unclosed or empty
    interpolations. Neighbouring errors are merged.
  - Linter corrections:
    - a selector ending in > is now flagged;
    - members beside $reactiveRoot are linted rather than warned about;
    - two directives in one member's record are reported once;
    - $compute placed at record level is called "not a directive of a layer
      record" rather than "unknown".

● An identical redefinition doesn't re-render a live view, checked in Chromium.
  I added this as a new test in
  tests/framework-tests/components/js/LiveExampleTests.js; the page now passes 5
  of 5, and lint is clean.

  The test sets up two instances of one view layer:
  - Inside the example: the example's code defines the layer, and its view at
    the left renders a label that a $compute produces and counts.
  - Elsewhere on the page: a second instance of the same layer is created
    outside the example, as another example's would be.

  An edit that leaves the record unchanged. I added a comment, so the code
  reruns and redefines the layer with an identical new record:
  - The label is computed exactly once more, by the example's own new instance.
    The instance elsewhere doesn't recompute.
  - The instance elsewhere keeps the same DOM element, so its markup isn't
    re-rendered.

  A real change. I then changed the record's name. The instance elsewhere
  re-renders with the new text, which shows the test can detect a re-render.

● All four issues are fixed, tested and checked in Chromium. Rerun the build to
  pick them up; nothing is committed.

  Console and preview.
  - Every live example now has a small console panel underneath, titled
    "Console", which shows "No output" until something is logged.
  - An html live example that is a Single File Component is loaded with
    fluid.loadSFCText, and its preview appears at the left. The counter example
    in fluid-view shows "Clicked 0 times +1", and clicking it works. Editing the
    SFC refreshes the preview.
  - The console couldn't print an unavailable value, which showed up as an error
    mentioning unavailable.causes.map. That was a bug in my widget, not in
    Infusion, and it's fixed.

  Runnable versus syntax examples. Fences are now marked either live or syntax.
  A live example is editable, runs, and has its console and preview. A syntax
  example is read-only: still highlighted and linted, but never run and with no
  console. I decided which is which by running every example in Chromium. Only
  those that ran without errors and showed something stayed live:

  ┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬────────┐
  │         Page         │             Live              │ Syntax │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼────────┤
  │ Integration Language │ 6                             │ 29     │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼────────┤
  │ Fluid View           │ 3 (including the SFC counter) │ 28     │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼────────┤
  │ Layer Linearisation  │ 1                             │ 2      │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼────────┤
  │ Signals, PTF, tldraw │ 0                             │ all 8  │
  └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┴────────┘

  So 10 examples are live and 67 are syntax. Many examples only define layers,
  or rely on layers they never define (my.toolbar, my.editor…), so they
  demonstrate nothing when run. Eleven lines that stated a result as a comment,
  like r.area; // 12, now print it with console.log, so those examples show
  their result. I rewrote the note at the top of each page to explain the two
  kinds.

  Error messages and fixes. No error is reported as a bare "Syntax error" any
  more. Each message says what's wrong, and a proposed fix appears as a button
  in the gutter tooltip. In Chromium, I removed a comma from a live example. The
  tooltip read Syntax error - expected "," between the members of an object
  with an Insert "," button, and clicking it fixed the code and reran the
  example. Fixes are offered for:
  - JavaScript:
    - missing commas between members, array elements or call arguments;
    - ; or = used inside an object;
    - unterminated strings;
    - unclosed brackets (it names the line where the open bracket is),
      mismatched brackets and extra closing brackets;
    - a dotted key, by quoting it;
    - == written in a declaration.
  - Inside configuration strings:
    - unclosed references, calls and interpolations;
    - empty arguments;
    - a missing : after $compute, or a missing . after };
    - a literal $ that needs escaping;
    - quoted arguments;
    - text after a complete reference.
  - Misspellings: "did you mean …?", with a fix, for directives and keys, e.g.
    $comptue, $layer, arg, valuesAs, inputLayer.

  The "ie" warning. It came from ponder's theme, not Infusion.
  beautifulWend-head.vue had an obsolete <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" 
  content="IE=edge">, and Chrome complains when booting the page rewrites its
  content. I removed the tag, and the docs pages now load with no warnings.
