  What I added to each converted example:
  - Small stand-in layers or functions for whatever it referred to but never
    defined, for example my.catalogue and my.searchBox for the injection
    example. The socket example uses fake my.openSocket/my.closeSocket functions
    that log, so you can see it open, rebind and close.
  - A few closing lines that create the component and log the result. The
    expected output is in comments next to each console.log.

  The newly live examples:
  - Integration Language:
    - composite $effect chain;
    - injection;
    - borrowing a view, previewed at the left;
    - removing a subcomponent;
    - keyed $for ordered by priority;
    - layerAs;
    - writing through valueAs;
    - linking one member of a reactive root;
    - $linkage;
    - $bindable;
    - fluid.liveQueryILSelector.
  - Fluid View: partial templates, previewed as a dated header without its
    strapline.
  - Layer Linearisation: the boat hierarchy, which logs pedalo's linearisation
    strongest first.
  - Signals: elementwise equality, and the untracked history.
  - PTF: the counter panel, which logs its PTF document. my.counter is defined
    in JavaScript there, because the original is loaded from an SFC. A comment
    says so.

  I also updated the intro notes on the Signals and PTF pages, which said all
  their examples were read-only.

  Widget bug fixed (fluid-liveExample.vue): the widget picks which layer to
  preview by checking whether the layer's own definition has a view. A layer
  that only inherits its view was skipped. In the partial-template example it
  previewed my.header.bare instead, a layer that only adjusts a view, so the
  preview was empty. It now also checks the layer's ancestors, and ignores
  layers that only adjust an inherited view.

  Layer name clash: two live Integration Language examples defined my.app with
  different contents, so I renamed the second one to my.inbox. No other layer is
  defined differently by two live examples on the same page.

  - examples that need data that is only filled in when the page is built;
  - the tldraw widgets, which need the tldraw app;
  - my.patternedMap, which depends on my.map from the example before it;
  - the popup example, which needs real page elements.

  SFMono-Regular, SF Mono, Menlo, Consolas, Liberation Mono, monospace) in their
  code editors. I added one CSS rule to
  src/components/sfc/fluid-liveExample.vue.

    would override a plain rule. My selector, .fl-live-example-source .cm-editor
    .cm-scroller, is more specific, so it wins.
  - Code before the editor loads: the same rule covers the plain code shown
    before the editor starts, so the font doesn't change as the page boots.

● The my.type.default example now gives the same result after every edit: Page,
  then Blog post.

  Cause: a rerun started with the layers the previous run had defined still in
  place. So my.type.post already existed before the code got to the point of
  defining it.

  Fix: I fixed this in the widget rather than in the docs example, since any
  example that defines a layer partway through would trip over the same thing.
  In fluid-liveExample.vue, before each rerun:
  - The widget remembers which layers the code first defined itself, as opposed
    to ones that already existed on the page. Before rerunning, it deletes those
    with fluid.deleteLayer, so the rerun starts from the same layers as the
    first run.
  - It keeps any such layer that a component outside the example still uses,
    such as another example's view. Redefining that layer identically still
    leaves those components untouched, and the existing test for that still
    passes.

  I ran into one catch along the way: destroy() only takes effect when the graph
  next stabilises, so the widget now stabilises after destroying the previous
  run's components and before choosing what to delete.

● I've made all six changes to the inspector, and checked each in the running
  tldraw demo with a storyTime widget beside an inspector. Lint is clean and
  Infusion's npm test passes 2591/2591, but that suite has no inspector tests,
  so the demo check is all that covers these changes.

  Containment graph not updating (the real bug). The graph only refreshed when a
  whole widget was added to or removed from the canvas. It ignored changes
  inside the inspected widget. With an empty story, imageGen and segmentList are
  grey placeholders, and once you typed, the graph still showed them that way.
  So selecting them always gave an empty hierarchy, which looked like the
  selection wasn't working. The inspector now watches the widget's components
  with fluid.liveQueryILSelector. Once the story has text, the graph shows the
  three segmentList members as fluid.demos.storySegment and imageGen as
  fluid.demos.storyImageGen. Selecting each shows its hierarchy.

  Anchor line. A dashed line runs from the point on the inspector's border
  nearest the inspected widget's centre, to that centre, with a small circle at
  each end. It moves with panning and zooming, sits above the shapes, and
  ignores clicks. It's hidden when there's nothing to inspect, or when the
  widget's centre is inside the inspector. tldraw clips every widget to its
  shape, so the inspector can't draw outside itself. So I added a small drawing
  layer to the canvas, in tldraw-driver.js and tldraw-hosting.js, which any
  widget can draw on.

  Grey components open where they're defined. Selecting a component with no user
  layers opens the tab of the layer that defines it inline. The editor scrolls
  there and selects the definition. It uses the same defMaps lookup as
  fluid-editor, loaded by the inspector itself. For example:
  - segmentList opens its $component record in fluid.demos.storyTime.
  - A view that comes from its SFC's <template> opens that <template>.

  The hierarchy pane names the defining layer. If the editor hasn't loaded yet,
  it scrolls once it has.

  Smaller changes:
  - View components now appear in the containment graph, inside a dashed grey
    ring.
  - The root is labelled /.
  - The editor uses the font stack you gave.

  Graph labels: showing views roughly doubles the number of nodes in the
  containment graph. The graph is scaled down to fit, so its labels are now
  quite small. If that bothers you, I could space nodes more tightly or draw
  views closer to their components.

● I've fixed four of your five points, and there's a new browser test for the
  inspector that passes. The anchor offset is the exception: I couldn't
  reproduce it in headless Chromium.

  Anchor line:
  - It's now solid blue.
  - In every setup I tried, both ends land exactly where they should, measured
    in screen pixels. I tried the default camera, a pan with zoom 0.6, a 1.5×
    display scale, and dragging the inspector. A screenshot looks right too.
  - To rule out stylesheet scoping, the line's position no longer depends on the
    SFC's stylesheet: the svg now carries its positioning inline.
  - If you still see the offset, please tell me the browser, the tldraw zoom
    level and your display scaling, and whether it happens straight away or only
    after panning, zooming or resizing.

  Clicks on the containment and hierarchy panes: tldraw was taking the mouse
  press to select or drag the shape, so the graphs never received the click.
  Widgets only got clicks on elements whose handlers come from their template,
  and the graph listeners are attached directly in code. I added a class,
  fl-tldraw-interactive, which tldraw-hosting.js now treats as interactive, and
  put it on both panes. The new test fails at the first graph click without this
  fix and passes with it.

  Root label: the root is now labelled with the nickname of its most derived
  layer, e.g. helloWorld, or / if it has no user layers.

  Broken layers: I reproduced this. Naming an undefined parent layer made the
  widget unavailable, and the inspector dropped all its tabs and editors. Now an
  unavailable widget still shows its root node and every layer it can find, all
  editable, with the reason in the title. When you fix the text, the widget and
  its full tree come back, and the editor stays put throughout. Two limits:
  - It finds the layers that were in use the last time the widget worked, plus
    the shape's layer and its user ancestors.
  - A widget that has never worked shows only that ancestor chain, and the tree
    below the root isn't shown while the widget is broken.

  Tests: the new script is demo/tldraw/inspector-script.json, added to
  infusion.tests.browser in package.json. It drives the real demo with real
  mouse and keyboard input:
  1. Creates an inspector from the layer picker, next to Hello World.
  2. Checks the root label, the ring around the view, and the tab.
  3. Drags the inspector away and checks the anchor ends: one on Hello World's
     centre, the other on the inspector's edge.
  4. Clicks the view node and checks it's reported as declared in
     fluid.demos.helloWorld, with its <template> selected in the editor.
  5. Clicks the root and then the hierarchy node, and checks the hierarchy shows
     the layer and its tab is active. Hello World has only one layer and one
     tab, so this step can't yet prove a click switches tabs.
  6. Types a broken parent layer name into the editor, then repairs it, checking
     the editor survives and the widget comes back.

  To support this, the shared test helpers (demo-agent.js and demo-runner.js)
  gained a drag action, CodeMirror 6 editing, and two position checks: centred
  on an element, and centre lying on an element's edge.

  npm run lint is clean and npm run test:browser passes all 43 steps across the
  three demo scripts. I didn't re-run npm test this round; these changes don't
  touch anything it covers. Nothing is committed.

  The next useful test would inspect storyTime, to check grey $component
  members, several tabs, and that hierarchy clicks really switch tabs. Its
  New-shape placement has a random nudge, so it needs a fixed setup first.

  such as a 109 version of Chrome, for which there was a puppeteer driver

  symmetric algorithm where the inspector and target are joined by the closest  
  pair out of their 8 points which consist of their corners and edge midpoints. 
  When the CodeMirror editor has focus, make sure that scroll-wheel gestures

  arena. Use the fluid-lint infrastructure developed for wend to highlight      
  line-precise errors in the CodeMirror gutter rather than just showing the "1  
  problem" marker on the widget.

● I've made all four changes. Lint is clean, npm test passes 2591/2591, and npm 
  run test:browser passes 43/43 steps across the three demo scripts. One gap:
  the Chrome 109 offset still doesn't occur in puppeteer's headless Chrome 109,
  so I haven't confirmed the fix in the browser where you saw it.

  Anchor routing in older browsers: The old line was drawn in a 1×1 svg that let
  its content spill outside its own box. My best guess is that Chrome 109
  misplaces content drawn outside an svg's bounds inside tldraw's transformed
  layer. The svg is now positioned and sized to just cover the line, with a
  small margin for the end circles, so nothing is drawn outside its own box.
  Could you check it in your Chrome 109?

  Closest-pair routing: each shape offers 8 points, its corners and edge
  midpoints. The line joins the closest pair, treating the inspector and the
  target the same way, and it's hidden while the shapes overlap. The test now
  checks that each end lies on its shape's edge.

  Scroll wheel: while an inspector editor has focus, the wheel scrolls the
  editor instead of panning the canvas. I checked this with real wheel events on
  the storyTime layer:
  - Unfocused, the wheel still pans the canvas (the camera moved 200px).
  - Focused, the editor scrolled 200px and the camera didn't move.

  This is checked in a scratch script, not in the committed test script, because
  Hello World's layer is too short to scroll.

  Problems in the gutter:
  - fluid-lint: fluidEditor in packages/fluid-lint/src/codemirror.js has a new
    extraDiagnostics option, shown alongside fluid-lint's own diagnostics, plus
    a relint(view) export to refresh them. I rebuilt
    src/lib/fluid-lint/fluid-lint.js.
  - The inspector: it gets the widget's problems from the same diagnosis that
    drives the badge. Each problem is underlined and marked in the gutter where
    the layer's text first mentions a name in the message. For example, "Layer
    fluid.topLevelWidgetZ is not defined" is underlined at
    fluid.topLevelWidgetZ.
  - Problems with no name in the text are marked on line 1 of the widget's own
    layer, which is less precise. One such case: when an SFC's script fails to
    run, the evaluation error can only be placed on <script>. fluid-lint already
    marks the syntax error at its exact position.

  Tests: in demo/tldraw/inspector-script.json, the "break the layer" step now
  expects one gutter marker, with the underline exactly on
  fluid.topLevelWidgetZ. The repair step expects the marker to clear. In
  demo-agent.js, a check on an element inside a CodeMirror 6 editor now reads
  that element's own text rather than the whole document.

  dist/src/lib/fluid-lint/ still has the old bundle; your usual dist build will
  update it. Nothing is committed.

  - Copy as → PTF writes the selection to the clipboard as a PTF document.

  How it hooks in: tldraw has no way to add items to its built-in "Copy as" and
  "Export as" submenus. So in tldraw-driver.js I rebuilt the context menu from
  tldraw's exported pieces, in the same order as its default, with the two
  submenus gaining PTF. The two actions and their "PTF" labels are added through
  tldraw's overrides. Their helpers are in tldraw-clipboard.js, and use the
  same encoding as copying a widget with Ctrl+C.

  Points to know:

    videos, depends on a check tldraw doesn't export. I recreated it as: any
    selected image or video that has an asset.

    default context menu won't show up here until this copy is updated.

    Adding them to inspector-script.json would need a right-click action in the
    test runner.

● Yes, that's done. The mouse wheel now scrolls an inspector editor whenever the
  pointer is over it, with or without focus, instead of panning the canvas. I
  checked it with real wheel events on storyTime's long layer:
  - Unfocused, wheel down 200: the editor scrolled 200px and the canvas didn't
    move.
  - Ctrl+wheel over the editor: tldraw zoomed as usual, to 90%.
  - Focused: the editor scrolls, as before.

  When the wheel still goes to the canvas (only while the editor doesn't have
  focus; a focused editor keeps the gesture even at its edge):
  - When Ctrl or Cmd is held, so zooming works everywhere.
  - When the editor can't scroll any further in that direction, for example when
    its text fits or it's already at the end. Without this, a short layer would
    block panning across a large patch of the canvas.

  I didn't check the case where the editor is already at its end and the wheel
  passes on to tldraw; that rests on reading the code.

  The rule is in fluid.demos.inspector.routeWheel in fluid-demos-inspector.vue,
  and only affects the inspector's editors.

  Lint is clean and npm run test:browser still passes 49/49, though no test
  covers the wheel. Nothing is committed.

  - The upper pane keeps at least 80px and the lower pane at least 120px.
  - In fluid-demos-inspector.vue, the bar is added as a fluid.resizeBar
    subcomponent. Its layer is mapped in the inspector's $importMap, so the
    inspector no longer relies on the page having loaded it.

  Two changes outside the inspector made this work:
  - tldraw-hosting.js: resize bars are now among the elements that receive their
    own pointer gestures. Without this, tldraw would take the drag and move the
    shape.
  - fluid-resizeBar.vue (the shared component): inside a zoomed canvas, the bar
    measured the panes in on-screen pixels but the space they share in unzoomed
    pixels. At zoom 0.6, for example, it would have moved the wrong distance. It
    now measures both on screen. Where nothing is scaled, the two measurements
    are equal, so its behaviour elsewhere is unchanged.

  The 2px ridge is set only on the demo's two bars: #ai-resize-bar in
  index.html, and .fl-resize-bar inside the inspector's own styles. The standard
  default stays 4px, which still affects the full-page editor. If you'd rather
  make 2px the default everywhere, I can change it in fluid-resizeBar.vue

● Yes, the inspector's target widget now gets the same blue outline tldraw gives
  a shape under the mouse. I checked it in the browser:
  - Moving the inspector: with Hello World and a counter on the canvas, the
    outline was on Hello World first. After I moved the inspector nearer the
    counter, it switched to the counter, and the screenshot shows it there.
  - Deleting the inspector: the outline disappeared.

  How it works: tldraw only tracks one hovered shape, set by the mouse, so
  pointing it at the target would be overwritten as soon as the mouse moved.
  Instead:
  - The outline: tldraw 5.5 draws its selection and hover outlines with a
    built-in ShapeIndicatorOverlayUtil, which a page can replace with its own
    version. In tldraw-driver.js, I added a subclass that also draws the target
    shapes with the same colour and line width.
  - When it shows: only at the moments a hover outline would show, while the
    select tool is idle. So it's hidden mid-drag or while a style is being
    changed.
  - Marking the target: fluid.tldraw.markShape and fluid.tldraw.unmarkShape mark
    and unmark a shape. They keep a count per shape, so with two inspectors on
    the same widget, the outline stays until neither targets it.
  - The inspector: it has a new markTarget member that marks its target and
    follows it as the target changes.

  Caveat: this depends on tldraw replacing a built-in overlay when a custom one
  has the same type. That holds in 5.5.2 but isn't a documented guarantee, so a
  tldraw upgrade could undo it without any error.

  Lint is clean and npm run test:browser passes 49/49. No test covers the
  outline yet. Nothing is committed.

● The publish was refused because the package included hard-linked files, and a
  dry-run pack now passes cleanly. More urgently, the same package also
  contained your private keys and passwords. The registry rejected the entire
  upload, so none of them reached npm.

  Why it happened: if a project has a .npmignore, npm uses it instead of
  .gitignore, not as well. So nothing excluded by .gitignore was excluded from
  the package. That pulled in:
  - Two copies of node_modules: packages/fluid-lint/node_modules and
    extension/codemirror/node_modules. Each contains esbuild's binary twice as a
    hard link, which is what the registry refuses.
  - Secrets:
    - pixabay-api-key.txt
    - ifm-password.txt
    - cavi-key.txt
    - demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json
    - docs/demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json

  The fix: I added node_modules/ (at any depth) and those five secret files to
  .npmignore, with a note that .gitignore's exclusions have to be repeated
  there.

  Check: npm pack --dry-run now lists 714 files instead of 1234, and the package
  is 5.5 MB instead of 16.9 MB. No node_modules or secret files are left, and
  none of the remaining files is a hard link. You can retry npm publish.

  demo/tldraw/js/tldraw-credentials.js, and its copy under docs/, is still in
  the package because git tracks it. If it holds a real tldraw licence key, it's
  already public in the repository. Its own comments call it gitignored, so it
  may have been committed by mistake.

● It arose now because the secret files only reached this checkout the day after
  6.3.0 was published. Nothing about the packing changed.

  1. .npmignore has always been the only exclusion list. When a project has one,
     npm uses it instead of .gitignore, and this project has had one since May.
     Every git-ignored file was therefore always eligible to be packed, and it
     was only safe while none existed.
  2. The secrets arrived on 18 November. The checkout was created on 6 November,
     and 6.3.0 was published from it on 17 November at 13:56. The files'
     creation times show they were added on 18 November between 14:10 and 14:17:
     - cavi-key.txt
     - ifm-password.txt
     - pixabay-api-key.txt
     - demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json

     Their modified times all read 23 October, which suggests they were copied
     from elsewhere with their original times kept. That's why they look older
     than the 6.2.x releases, which they weren't part of.
  3. This was the first publish attempt since. The fluid-lint build here
     regenerated docs/demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json today, copying the CAVI key into
     docs/. The publish would have shipped all five files.
  4. The hard links came the same way. extension/codemirror/node_modules
     appeared on 19 November and packages/fluid-lint/node_modules on 21
     November. Both are new, so their hard-linked esbuild binaries were also
     packed for the first time, and the registry rejected the whole upload. That
     rejection is what stopped the secrets going out.

  Earlier releases were packed from this same working tree: 6.3.0 includes notes
  that git doesn't track, such as FLUID-7037.md. So they would have shipped the
  keys if the files had been present then.

  One related item: every release since 6.2.0 includes
  .claude/settings.local.json, which is tracked in git. It's only 174 bytes and
  contains no keys or tokens, but it's a local settings file that probably
  shouldn't be in the package. I can add it to .npmignore alongside today's fix

❯ When was .npmignore added to the project? Would it be safer rather than       
  .npmignore to use opt-in in package.json using "files"?                       

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● .npmignore was added on 15 May 2026, in commit df7b522 ("Added copy button to
  code-box … removed npm prepare so that we could make a clean publish"). That
  was four days after 6.0.0 was published on 11 May. So 6.0.0 was packed under
  .gitignore, and every release from 6.1.0 on has been packed under .npmignore
  alone.

  Yes, an opt-in "files" list in package.json would be safer. With .npmignore,
  anything new in the working tree gets published unless someone remembers to
  exclude it. That is how today's keys and nested node_modules got in, along
  with untracked notes like FLUID-7037.md in 6.3.0. With "files", only what's
  listed is published, and a new stray file is left out by default.

  Two catches:
  - .npmignore stops protecting you. With "files" present, the root .npmignore
    can't remove anything from the listed folders, though an .npmignore inside a
    subfolder still can. So if docs is listed, docs/demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json
    would be published unless you exclude it in "files" itself, e.g.
    "!docs/demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json", or keep generated keys out of published
    folders altogether. Excluding node_modules at every depth should also be
    written into "files".
  - You have to decide what the package is for. Today's package contains 23
    top-level entries: src, dist, bin, tests, docs, demo, extension, packages,
    and build scripts such as build.js, render.js, es6-bundle.js and
    deploySnippet.js. Some are probably there by accident.

  Fairly clearly needed:
  - src (holds main)
  - bin (the three fluid-* commands)
  - dist
  - tests/package.json, plus tests/test-core and the test suites, since
    fqunit-cli.js reads them for projects that test against the package

  package.json, README.md and LICENSE are always included anyway.

  Your call: docs, demo, extension, packages, the build scripts, tsconfig.json,
  AGENTS.md and .puppeteerrc.cjs.

  I'd keep the current .npmignore as a backstop either way. Tell me which of
  those last items should ship and I'll write the "files" list, then check it
  with npm pack --dry-run against what 6.3.0 contained.

  earlier build had left at docs/demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json. I haven't run a full
  build to confirm the change end to end.

  Cause: the build copies all of demo/ into docs/ file by file, and that copy
  doesn't honour .gitignore. So demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json went with it. The
  .gitignore entry for the docs/ copy only kept it out of git. It didn't stop
  the file being deployed to GitHub Pages from docs/, or packed by npm.

  Fix: build.js now has a secretFiles list: cavi-key.json, cavi-key.txt,
  ifm-password.txt and pixabay-api-key.txt. Every copy into docs/ and dist/
  skips any file with one of those names, including the copies of src and tests.
  I updated the comment in .gitignore to match, and kept its entry for the
  docs/ copy in case an old build leaves one behind.

  Checks:
  - node --check and lint pass.
  - I didn't run build.js itself, since it deletes and regenerates all of docs/.
    Instead I ran the same file filter over demo/**: it excluded exactly
    demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json.

  The local copy in demo/tldraw/ stays, because the demo fetches the key from
  there when served locally.

  Still worth checking: whether any earlier build's
  docs/demo/tldraw/cavi-key.json reached GitHub Pages. It was git-ignored and so
  shouldn't have been committed. But if your Pages deployment publishes docs/
  from the working tree rather than from git, the key may have been served.

  The .npmignore additions from earlier are still in place, so check them before
  you back out the commit. Nothing is committed.

● The target's outline now sits at the target's own place in the stacking order,
  so the inspector covers it where they overlap. In the browser, with the
  inspector placed over part of the counter, the screenshot shows the blue
  outline going under the inspector. A check of what's visible at the overlapped
  edge found the inspector, not the outline.

  The outline fix (tldraw-driver.js): tldraw draws all its outlines on a single
  layer above every shape, which is why the old outline floated over the
  inspector. So I removed my replacement of tldraw's outline layer. The outline
  is now a thin blue line inside the target's own shape, which tldraw stacks
  like any other shape.

  It looks as before:
  - tldraw's selection colour, 1.5 screen pixels wide at any zoom, shown only
    while the select tool is idle;
  - marking still works through fluid.tldraw.markShape and
    fluid.tldraw.unmarkShape, so the inspector itself is unchanged.

  One small difference: tldraw's own outlines are centred on the shape's edge,
  while this one sits just inside it, since shapes clip anything drawn outside
  them.

  A second bug, found while testing: placing an inspector next to a widget still
  being built sometimes showed "is not available – it could not be inspected",
  and it never recovered. This had nothing to do with the outline; it depended
  on timing.
  - Cause: while the widget is being built, some of its parts don't exist yet;
    here it was the counter's view. The framework's fluid.ptf.componentToParts
    fails on them, and the failure left the inspector watching nothing that
    would make it try again.
  - Fix (in the inspector): it now skips parts that aren't built yet, but
    watches for them, so they appear once ready. It also takes its list of
    layers from the parts it has already visited, instead of calling
    componentToParts.
  - Check: the failure happened in two of three runs before the fix, and in none
    of five runs after. The counter's tree now shows counter and view.

  componentToParts itself still fails on a widget that's only partly built, so
  copying such a widget as PTF could hit the same error. That's a fix for
  FluidPTF.js in the core framework, which I've left alone; say if you'd like me
  to make it.

  Lint is clean and npm run test:browser passes 49/49. Nothing is committed.

● I've fixed fluid.ptf.componentToParts in FluidPTF.js. It no longer fails on a
  widget that's only partly built, which covers copying such a widget as PTF.

  Cause: a parent records its child components before they're built, and a child
  gets its component only when it's first evaluated. In the browser this left
  the counter's view without a component while its template loaded.
  componentToParts read each child's layers from its component, so it failed on
  any child in that state.

  Fix: for a child that hasn't been built yet, the layers are now read from its
  potentia. The potentia is already there and holds the same layer names;
  componentToParts already reads the root's layers this way. The rest of what it
  packs (the potentia and live layer of each component) never needed the built
  component.

  Test: in FluidPTFTests.js I added "Subcomponent still being constructed is
  transmitted from its potentia":
  - It builds a parent with one child and calls componentToParts before the
    graph has settled, when the child has a shadow but no component.
  - It checks that both layers are packed, and that the same layers come out
    after the child is built.
  - With the old line put back, this test fails (206 of 207 passed); with the
    fix, all 208 tests in that file pass.

  Lint is clean, npm test passes 2594/2594, and npm run test:browser passes
  49/49.

  The inspector's own workaround from the last change stays in place: it reads
  layers from the components it has already visited. That still holds now that
  componentToParts is fixed. I can switch it back to calling componentToParts if
  you'd rather keep a single code path.

  Nothing is committed.

● The plugin is in packages/eslint-plugin-fluid-lint/, and npm run lint now runs
  fluid-lint over the whole project, including the .vue files. ESLint had never
  been checking those, because the lint script only looked at .js files. The
  project lints clean.

  What the plugin gives you:
  - Two rules: fluid-lint/errors and fluid-lint/warnings carry fluid-lint's
    findings at each severity. You can configure them or silence them with an
    eslint-disable comment like any other rule.
  - Processor for SFCs: fluid-lint/vue checks each SFC's top-level <script> and
    its <template>. ESLint doesn't parse the SFC itself, so other rules still
    don't apply to those files.
  - Config: plugin:fluid-lint/recommended turns on both rules and the processor.
  - Fixes: a fix fluid-lint proposes, such as inserting a missing }, is offered
    as a suggestion your editor can apply. eslint --fix won't apply it, because
    it's a guess at what was meant.
  - It loads fluid-lint's ES module directly, which needs Node 22.12 or later
    (you're on 26).

  Applied to the project:
  - .eslintrc.json extends plugin:fluid-lint/recommended.
  - The lint script passes --ext .js,.vue.
  - The plugin is a dev dependency installed from the folder
    (file:packages/eslint-plugin-fluid-lint). Installing it edited
    package-lock.json: it added the link and brought the lockfile's stale
    version (6.2.6) up to 6.4.0.
  - npm re-sorted dependencies in package.json during the install; I put the
    original order back.

  Fixes to fluid-lint itself: a first pass over the 131 files found just two
  problems, both false alarms in fluid-lint:
  - $component: null was flagged, but it legitimately removes a component.
  - $layers: layerName was flagged, but a value held in a variable can't be
    checked without running the code.

  fluid-lint now flags only plain values that can never be valid there, such as
  numbers, booleans and object literals, and I added a test for each case.

  Checks:
  - The plugin's own tests pass 14/14.
  - fluid-lint's tests pass 180/180.
  - Broken text piped through npx eslint --stdin under the project config is
    reported for both .js and .vue.
  - npm test passes 2594/2594.

  Decision for you: the new plugin folder isn't excluded from .npmignore, so it
  would be published to npm along with fluid-lint, which already is. Should I

● There's no app code to write or host. A GitHub App is a registration in your
  GitHub settings. What it gives the extension is a public client id, and the
  extension does the rest. Only the Edit in Infusion extension
  (extension/edit-in-infusion/) talks to GitHub; wend's build doesn't.

  The app sign-in isn't built yet. The extension still asks for a token you
  paste in: a fine-grained personal access token with Contents: read and write,
  saved in its options page. My earlier "no Worker" point was a design note in
  a-scratch/reports/0-live-static-editing.md §3.10. The device flow it describes
  hasn't been implemented. For now you could just paste a token and skip the
  app.

  Registering the app, at github.com → Settings → Developer settings → GitHub
  Apps → New GitHub App:
  1. Name and homepage: e.g. "Edit in Infusion"; the homepage can be the ponder
     site.
  2. Callback URL: leave it empty, and leave "Request user authorization (OAuth)
     during installation" off. The device flow doesn't redirect anywhere.
  3. Enable Device Flow: tick it. This is what removes the need for a secret,
     and so for a Worker.
  4. Webhook: untick Active, since nothing needs to receive events.
  5. Repository permissions: Contents: Read and write. Metadata: Read is added
     automatically. Leave everything else off; in particular, it shouldn't share
     permissions with the curation app.
  6. "Expire user authorization tokens": untick it. Renewing an expiring token
     needs the client secret, which the extension can't hold.
  7. Where it can be installed: Only on this account is enough for ponder.
     Choose Any account if other people should edit their own sites with it.
  8. Create it and note the Client ID (Iv23…). It's safe to ship inside the
     extension. Don't generate a client secret or private key; neither is
     needed.
  9. Install it: on the app's page, choose Install App, pick your account and
     select only amb26/ponder, the repo named in infusion/linkage.json. Repeat
     for each site repository you want to edit.

  What the extension still needs, once you have the client id:
  - Add https://github.com/* to host_permissions in its manifest. The background
    script needs it to call the device-code and token endpoints, which don't
    allow cross-origin calls from pages.
  - Add a "Sign in with GitHub" step to the options page in place of the
    paste-in box. It would show the code, link to github.com/login/device, poll
    for the token, and store it under githubToken as now. js/github.js needs no
    changes, since a token issued to the app is used the same way as a personal
    one.
  - Update the README and STORE.md; the new host permission needs a
    justification for the Chrome Web Store.

  Once you've registered the app and have its client id, I can implement that
  sign-in, with the mock GitHub in extension/test extended to cover it.

❯ The UI doesn't let me leave the Callback URL (it calls it "Redirect URI")     
  blank - it says that at least one is required. Also, think about this         
  workflow "in the wild" - it seems that I personally or some such person need

● The Redirect URI. Put in any URL you control, such as the ponder site's
  homepage, e.g. https://ponder.org.uk/. The device flow never redirects, so
  nothing will ever be sent to it.

  Enlisting repositories "in the wild". The person enlisting a repository is
  that repository's owner, not you. If you set the app's install option to Any 
  account, it gets a public page at https://github.com/apps/<app-name>. Any site
  owner can install it there on the repositories they choose, without you being
  involved. Your part is only the one-time registration.

  What can't be made unattended is the owner's consent. GitHub requires the
  account or organisation owner to approve every installation, and to approve
  its permissions again if you widen them. That's deliberate: otherwise anyone
  could give their app write access to someone else's repo. In an organisation,
  a member who isn't an owner can only request the installation, and an owner
  then approves it.

  There are two ways to make this nearly frictionless:

  1. Send the user straight to the install page. When the extension finds it
     can't write to a site's repo, it can open the app's install page with that
     repository preselected. It knows the repo from the page's linkage record.
     The user then makes one confirmation click on GitHub and comes back. Given
     Any account, I think this is the best fit.
     - The install page accepts suggested_target_id and repository_ids[] query
       parameters for the preselection. I'm working from memory there and
       haven't checked GitHub's current docs; I'd verify before building on it.
  2. Use an OAuth App instead. An OAuth App, rather than a GitHub App, has no
     per-repository installation at all. It also supports the device flow, so
     still no Worker. The token the user signs in with can write to every
     repository that user can write to.
     - The cost is breadth: the public_repo or repo scope covers all of the
       user's repositories, not just the site.
     - Organisations with OAuth App restrictions turned on still need an owner
       to approve it once, organisation-wide.

  I'd keep the GitHub App, with its narrow Contents permission on chosen
  repositories, and add the direct link to the install page. A site author who
  wants their site editable already has to own or administer its repository, so
  one confirmation click on first use is a small cost.

  If you'd like, I can make that missing-installation flow part of the sign-in
  work: detect that the app isn't installed and offer the preselected install
  link.

● The OAuth App gets you to "one confirmation, then silence". After the first
  Authorize click, the extension can fork, create from a template, create a bare
  repository, fill it, and turn on Pages, all with nothing for the user to see
  on GitHub. Both options use GitHub's device flow, so neither needs a secret or
  a Worker, and both need a required-but-unused redirect URL. Points marked
  (verify) are from my memory of GitHub's behaviour; I haven't checked them
  against the docs.

  Option A: an OAuth App

  What the user sees, once:
  1. They click "Sign in with GitHub" in the extension, which shows an
     8-character code and opens github.com/login/device.
  2. They enter the code; GitHub shows "Authorize Edit in Infusion", listing the
     access requested. For the public_repo scope that reads roughly "Full
     control of public repositories" (verify).
  3. They click Authorize. That's it.

  Making a copy of a site:
  - The user names the copy in the extension and nothing appears on GitHub.
  - The extension forks (POST /repos/…/forks), generates from a template (POST 
    /repos/…/generate), or creates a bare repository (POST /user/repos) and
    writes the templated files as one commit.
  - It then turns on Pages from docs/ and waits for the site to appear.

  Costs:
  - Breadth: the token can write to every public repository the user can write
    to. Ask for repo only if private sites are needed, and workflow only if a
    template publishes through Actions.
  - Organisations: an organisation with OAuth App restrictions needs an owner to
    approve the app once (verify whether new organisations have this on by 
    default).
  - Upside: it works as it stands for a collaborator on someone else's site.

  Option B: a GitHub App

  What the user sees, once: two steps instead of one.
  1. Install the app on their account, choosing All repositories or Only select 
     repositories, then clicking Install.
  2. Authorize it with the same device-code steps as Option A.

  The extension can preselect the account and repository on the install page.

  Making a copy of a site:
  - With All repositories, it's silent, as in Option A.
  - With Only select repositories, a new fork or repository falls outside the
    installation. The token can create it but then can't write to it. The user
    has to visit GitHub's settings and add the repository by hand, at exactly
    the moment we want no formality.
  - It may be possible for the extension to add the repository to the
    installation through the API (verify). If so, that gap closes.

  Costs:
  - Narrower access: only installed repositories, and only the permissions
    granted (Contents, Administration, Pages).
  - Collaborators: someone editing another person's site needs that site's owner
    to have installed the app.

  Either way

  - Fork or template: a fork is limited to one per user, public if the original
    is, and tied to the original. A repository generated from a template can
    take any name, can be private, and has no tie. A template fits "start my own
    site"; a fork fits "propose a change".
  - Forks and Actions: a fork has GitHub Actions switched off until its owner
    turns them on (verify). Publishing Pages from a branch, as ponder does from
    docs/, doesn't need Actions, so this doesn't arise.
  - Timing: the extension should wait for a new repository's contents before
    writing to it, and for Pages to finish its first build. It can check the new
    site's fluid-trace.json the same way it already does for published edits.

  Recommendation: an OAuth App with public_repo, with the token's breadth stated
  plainly on the sign-in screen and in STORE.md. The GitHub App is only as
  frictionless if users choose All repositories. At that point its remaining
  advantage is finer-grained permissions, and it costs an extra step on first
  use.

  The write-up is saved as packages/wend/notes/github-sign-in.md in the ponder
  repo. It has more detail than this summary, including both registration forms
  and a side-by-side table. Nothing is committed.

● You're right on the first point: in Option B, the user has to install the app
  on their own account themselves, on GitHub's own pages. Neither the extension
  nor you as the app's maintainer can do it for them. The extension can only
  open the install page. There the user picks All repositories or Only select 
  repositories, reads the permissions list and clicks Install. That's a second
  visit to GitHub's UI on top of the Authorize page, and a fairly
  technical-looking one. I've reworded the notes to say so.

  Yes, the extension can turn on GitHub Pages itself. The user never needs to
  see GitHub's settings for it:
  - Turning it on: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pages, with {"source": {"branch": 
    "main", "path": "/docs"}}, publishes from a branch, as ponder does.
    {"build_type": "workflow"} would publish through GitHub Actions instead.
  - Tracking it: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pages gives the site's URL and
    status, and GET …/pages/builds/latest shows the first build's progress. The
    extension can show "your site is being published…" and then open the site.
  - Requirement: the user must be an admin of the repository, which they are of
    one they've just created.

  A catch for the OAuth App (verify): I believe GitHub's Pages endpoints require
  the full repo scope, even for a public repository, not just public_repo. If
  so, the extension should ask for repo at the first sign-in. Asking later would
  mean showing a second Authorize page exactly when the user is making their
  copy. But repo also covers private repositories, so the token becomes broader.
  A GitHub App needs only its Pages and Administration write permissions.

  Two other routes don't help:
  - A repository named <user>.github.io may publish without being asked
    (verify). It can only hold one site per user, at their root address.
  - A workflow in the template can't turn Pages on for its own repository,
    because its built-in token can't change the repository's settings (verify).

  What each option asks of the user in GitHub's UI:
  - OAuth App: one visit, the Authorize page on first sign-in. Creating, filling
    and publishing a site afterwards all happen inside the extension.
  - GitHub App: at least two visits, install and authorize. If the user picks
    Only select repositories, there's one more visit for each new site.

  For non-technical users this strengthens the case for the OAuth App. The cost
  to state plainly on the sign-in screen is that the token can write to all of
  the user's repositories, and possibly to private ones as well.

  I've updated packages/wend/notes/github-sign-in.md in the ponder repo with the
  install wording, a "Turning on GitHub Pages" section and two new comparison
  rows. Nothing is committed.

● I've built the "Sign in with GitHub" flow into the extension, using GitHub's
  sign-in for devices with an OAuth App. It works end to end against a mock of
  GitHub, but can't be used for real until you register the OAuth App and give
  me its client id. Until then the options page offers a pasted personal access
  token, as before.

  What a user sees:
  1. In the extension's options they click Sign in with GitHub, and a short code
     appears in large type.
  2. They click Copy code and open GitHub, paste the code into GitHub's page and
     click Authorize.
  3. The options page notices on its own and shows "Signed in as <their login>".

  How it works:
  - Background script (js/github.js): it asks GitHub for a code, then polls for
    the token, and handles:
    - GitHub asking it to poll more slowly;
    - the code expiring;
    - the user cancelling at GitHub.
  - Storage: the token is kept in the extension's own storage, along with the
    user's login. A sign-in still in progress is held in session storage, so it
    survives Chrome stopping the background script between polls.
  - Scope: it asks for public_repo only, which covers writing to the user's
    public repositories.
  - Options page: it now has sign-in, sign-out and cancel. The token box is
    still there, folded away under "Use a personal access token instead". It
    opens by itself when signing in isn't available.
  - Manifest: https://github.com/* is now among the host permissions, which the
    sign-in endpoints need. I've added its justification to STORE.md and updated
    the README.
  - Wording: the error shown when not signed in now reads "Not signed in to
    GitHub - sign in from the extension's options".

  Tests: I added extension/test/signin-scenario.js and a mock of GitHub's
  sign-in, including a stand-in for GitHub's code-entry page, which the test
  fills in like a user would. It covers:
  - signing in, including a request to slow down;
  - signing out;
  - cancelling at GitHub;
  - a copy with no client id, where the token fallback takes over.

  It passes 15/15. I added it to npm run test:extension, where the framing
  (24/24) and block-editor (32/32) scenarios also still pass. Lint is clean. I
  didn't re-run the changeset, drop, list and widget scenarios, which aren't
  part of test:extension.

  For you to do:
  1. Register the OAuth App at GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → OAuth 
     Apps (not GitHub Apps):
     - any homepage URL, and any callback URL you control, since it's never
       used;
     - tick Enable Device Flow;
     - don't generate a client secret.
  2. Give me the client id, or set it yourself as clientId in
     extension/edit-in-infusion/js/github.js.

  Still open: if GitHub's Pages API turns out to need the broader repo scope,
  scope in github.js will need changing before the create-a-site work. Users
  would then be asked for full access to private repositories too.

  Nothing is committed.

✻ Sautéed for 4m 25s · done Sunday 8:47 PM

❯ OK - where actually is the OAuth app - don't I need to actually host this     
  somewhere in e.g. a CloudFlare worker?                                        

● No, there's nothing to host. Despite the name, an "OAuth App" isn't a program.
  It's just a record you create in your GitHub settings, and all it gives you
  is a name, a client id, and the "Enable Device Flow" switch.

  All the code that runs is the extension's own, in js/github.js, inside the
  extension's background script on the user's machine. It talks to GitHub
  directly:
  1. It sends the client id to github.com/login/device/code, and GitHub replies
     with the code to show the user.
  2. The user approves it on GitHub's own page, github.com/login/device.
  3. The extension polls github.com/login/oauth/access_token with the client id
     until GitHub hands over the token.

  Why curation needed a Worker and this doesn't: two things normally force a
  server into GitHub sign-in, and neither applies here.
  - The client secret. The usual browser sign-in ends by trading a one-time code
    for a token. That trade needs the client secret, which can't be shipped in
    a page or an extension, so it has to happen on a server you control. The
    curation Worker exists for this. The device flow only needs the client id,
    which is public, so there's no secret to protect.
  - Cross-origin rules. GitHub's sign-in endpoints don't allow calls from web
    pages. An extension that holds the site as a host permission isn't bound by
    that rule, which is why I added https://github.com/* to the manifest.

  Where that would change: the extension can do this only because it's an
  extension. If wend ever lets people edit from an ordinary web page, with no
  extension installed, that page couldn't call GitHub's sign-in endpoints. It
  would need a small proxy, such as a Cloudflare Worker, even for the device
  flow. For the extension, registering the app and pasting its client id into
  github.js is all that's left.

✻ Sautéed for 13s · done Sunday 8:50 PM

❯ OK - I register the OAuth App - and then any GitHub user whatever can opt     
  into this workflow through the steps you mention at the "Sign in to GitHub"   
  point you described within the extension?                                     

● Yes. Once the app is registered with Enable Device Flow ticked, any GitHub
  user can sign in through the extension. You don't approve or enrol anyone, and
  there's nothing per user or per repository to set up. They go through the
  steps I described: the code, GitHub's page, Authorize.

  That gets them a sign-in, but what they can then edit has some limits:

  - They need a GitHub account. Someone without one has to create it on GitHub
    first. That's the one step on GitHub's site the extension can't do for them.
  - They can only edit repositories they can already write to. The token acts as
    the user, so it covers sites they own, plus any where the owner has added
    them as a collaborator. To edit someone else's site otherwise, they'd need
    their own copy, which is the fork and new-site feature not yet built.
  - Organisations can block the app. If a site's repository belongs to an
    organisation that restricts OAuth Apps, its repositories stay hidden from
    the token until an owner of that organisation approves the app once.
    GitHub's Authorize page lets the user request that approval.
  - Single sign-on organisations add a click. In an organisation that uses SAML
    single sign-on, GitHub may also ask the user to authorise the token for that
    organisation.
  - There may be a cap on sign-ins. I believe GitHub limits how many device-flow
    codes one app can request per hour, but I haven't checked the figure. It
    would only matter at large scale.

  The app being registered under your personal account doesn't limit who can use
  it. GitHub doesn't require OAuth Apps to be verified or approved before the
  public can use them. The Authorize page shows the app's name and that it's
  owned by you, so a clear name, logo and homepage on the registration will
  reassure people.

✻ Cooked for 12s · done Sunday 8:52 PM

❯ Do I want "Expire user access tokens"?                                        

● No, leave it unticked.

  If you tick it, each sign-in token stops working after about 8 hours, so users
  would have to go through the code and Authorize steps again every day.
  Expiring tokens come with a refresh token for renewing them silently. As far
  as I know, though, GitHub requires the client secret to use it, which brings
  back the server we avoided. The extension doesn't have any renewal code
  either.

  With it unticked, the token lasts until:
  - the user signs out in the options; that only forgets the token in their
    browser, while GitHub keeps it valid.
  - the user revokes the app in GitHub under Settings → Applications.
  - the token goes unused for about a year; I believe GitHub then revokes it,
    but haven't checked.

  What you give up is short-lived tokens limiting the damage if one leaks. The
  token is stored in the extension's own storage, which the pages being edited
  can't read. That's the usual setup for extensions using GitHub's device flow.

● I've set the client id (Ov23lignaxZLCR1CTDoX) in
  extension/edit-in-infusion/js/github.js and updated the README and STORE.md to
  match. Lint is clean, and nothing is committed.

  Why GitHub needed no configuration: the app doesn't do anything at GitHub.
  It's only an identity. It gives the extension a name to show on the Authorize
  page and a client id to quote when asking for a token. Everything that happens
  afterwards is the extension calling GitHub's ordinary API, using the token,
  as the user. GitHub never calls back into anything: there's no webhook, the
  callback URL is unused, and no code of yours runs on GitHub's side. In effect,
  the client id is the whole configuration.

  Next step: try it for real.
  1. In Chrome, open chrome://extensions and reload the unpacked extension. Load
     it unpacked first if it isn't installed yet.
  2. Open its Details → Extension options and click Sign in with GitHub.
  3. Click Copy code and open GitHub, paste the code and click Authorize.
     GitHub's page will show your app's name, the public_repo access, and you as
     its owner.
  4. The options page should then show "Signed in as amb26".
  5. Go to a page of the ponder site, click the extension's button, make a small
     edit and commit it. It should land on the ponder-infusion branch of
     amb26/ponder, and the extension will show when it's published.

  If you saved a personal access token earlier, signing in replaces it.

  While you're in the app's settings on GitHub, it's worth adding a logo and a
  description. Those are what other users will see on the Authorize page.

● I've added a welcome panel to the extension. Whenever you're not signed in, a
  left-click on its toolbar button opens it and walks you through connecting
  your GitHub account. Nobody needs to find the options page anymore.

  What the user sees:
  1. First click: a panel that says what the extension does and has one button,
     Connect my GitHub account. Beneath it is a "No GitHub account yet? Create
     one for free" link.
  2. After connecting: the panel shows a large code and three short numbered
     steps, with a Copy code and go to GitHub button. Pressing it copies the
     code and opens GitHub's page, which closes the panel. That's why the
     background script now does the waiting, not the panel.
  3. Once they click Authorize on GitHub: the extension brings them back to the
     tab they started from and puts a ✓ on its button. It also reopens the
     panel, which says "You're connected as …" with a Start editing this page
     button. Pressing that asks for access to the site and opens the editor.
  4. From then on: a click opens the editor directly, as before. Signing out
     brings the welcome panel back.

  The panel also has Cancel while waiting and a More options link to the options
  page. The options page shares the same sign-in: start it in either and the
  other shows it in progress.

  Things worth knowing:
  - Reopening the panel automatically works in Chrome 127 and later. In older
    versions, the ✓ badge is the prompt to click again.
  - In headless Chrome, openPopup() never finishes, so the extension no longer
    waits for it.
  - A test-build fix: an empty test client id is now honoured, rather than
    falling back to the real one. This let the test of a copy without a client
    id run again.

  Tests: the sign-in scenario now drives the panel as a page: connect, enter the
  code at the mock GitHub, return to the tab, start editing, sign out. It
  passes 24/24. npm run test:extension passes overall: sign-in 24/24, framing
  24/24 and block editor 32/32, and lint is clean. The headless tests can't
  click the real toolbar button or open the real popup, so give it a
  real-browser try. Reload the unpacked extension, pin it from the puzzle-piece
  menu, and click it on a ponder page.

  The new files are popup.html and js/popup.js. I also changed js/background.js,
  js/options.js, js/github.js, the README and
  extension/test/signin-scenario.js.

  Nothing is committed.

❯ I noticed when I was prompted by the extension that I was asked to trust      
  specifically "amb26" (my GitHub user account) with the OAuth app - is there a 
  way for this agency to be one of my organisations instead? I didn't seem to   
  see a way to attribute the OAuth App to an org when I created it              

● Yes, an organisation can own the app. You didn't see the choice because GitHub
  decides the owner by where you create the app, not with a setting on the
  form. You have two ways to do it:

  - Transfer the existing app (simplest). Open the app's settings (your Settings
    → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → the app) and look for Transfer 
    ownership. Enter the organisation's name and confirm. You need to be an
    owner of that organisation. I believe the client id and existing sign-ins
    carry over unchanged, so Ov23lignaxZLCR1CTDoX in js/github.js would keep
    working. I haven't checked that against GitHub's docs, so test a sign-in
    after transferring. If the id did change, send me the new one and I'll
    update it.
  - Register a fresh one under the organisation. Go to the organisation's
    Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New OAuth App, fill in the same
    form, and tick Enable Device Flow again. This gives a new client id, which
    I'd swap in, and anyone already signed in would have to sign in again.

  After either, GitHub's Authorize page will say the app is owned by the
  organisation rather than amb26. You can also add a logo and a description on
  the app's settings page, which make the Authorize page look more trustworthy.

  Owners of the organisation can manage the app too, so you're no longer the
  only one who can maintain it.

● Nothing was broken: you were still signed in, but my design left a left-click
  doing nothing visible. Reloading the extension cleared the stored "just signed
  in" step and the tick. From then on a left-click went straight to opening the
  editor, and on a page with nothing to edit, that only changes the button's
  tooltip. I loaded your copy fresh in Chrome 109: the background script starts
  cleanly and the right-click menu item exists.

  A left-click now always does something visible:
  - On a page the extension has recognised as editable, marked ✎, while you're
    signed in: the click opens the editor straight away, as before.
  - Anywhere else, the panel opens.
    - Signed out, it walks you through connecting your GitHub account,
      unchanged.
    - Signed in, it shows Connected to GitHub as amb26, an Edit this page button
      and a Sign out link. If the page has nothing to edit, it says so instead
      of doing nothing.
  - Right-click still offers Sign out of GitHub (amb26).

  The ✎ badge only appears on a site you've already allowed the extension to
  access, once one of its pages loads. Pressing Edit this page on a ponder page
  grants that access, and after that the ✎ shows on every page of the site. The
  ✓ tick appears only in the tab you came back to after signing in, and
  reloading the extension clears it.

  A fix this needed: the editor in the page never answered the "open the editor"
  message. The extension now uses that answer to tell whether a page had
  anything to edit, so the editor answers it.

  Checks: npm run test:extension passes: sign-in 27/27, framing 25/25 and block
  editor 32/32. Lint is clean. The new checks cover:
  - the panel opening when you're signed in;
  - Edit this page on a page with nothing to edit, which reports that and keeps
    the panel;
  - Sign out being offered in the panel;
  - a click on a recognised ponder page going straight to the editor.

  Please reload the extension and try a left-click on a ponder page and on some
  other page.

● The logo is back at full size, level with your other extensions' icons. The
  disc stays in its corner, one pixel bigger than your earlier version: 11px
  across at 16 (was 10), and 22px at 32 (was 20). It now covers slightly more of
  the logo, since it can't move outside the icon. If that's too much, I can go
  back to the 10px disc.

  The only way to have a mark hang below the logo is Chrome's native badge,
  which is what you saw first. The trade-off is that Chrome places the "✓"
  itself, about a pixel off-centre as you noticed, and I can't nudge it. A
  different tick character might sit better. I can't test the native badge's
  look headless, so you'd need to judge it.

  The panel changes you asked for are in place:
  - Every click opens the panel. It's now the default popup in the manifest; the
    click no longer opens the editor directly anywhere.
  - Signed in, the panel shows Edit this page. It's enabled only on a page with
    a Fluid linkage record. Elsewhere it's greyed out, and the tooltip reads
    "This page isn't editable - it wasn't built by a site which can be edited in
    place", or asks you to open a page of such a site.
  - Edit this page asks for access to the site, then opens the editor. On some
    platforms Chrome closes a popup while it shows a permission prompt. So the
    panel tells the background script which tab it means first, and the editor
    still opens when access is granted.
  - Sign out stays in the panel and in the right-click menu.

  npm run test:extension passed (sign-in 27/27, framing 25/25, block editor
  32/32) and lint is clean. That run was before your message; since then I've
  only changed how the icon is drawn, which those tests don't check, and lint is
  still clean.
  - Sign-in scenario: now checks the disabled button and its tooltip.
  - Framing scenario: now starts editing by pressing Edit this page in the
    panel, as you would.
  - Not covered headless: the real toolbar popup, the permission prompt, and how
    the icon looks at actual size. Please check those in your browser after
    reloading the extension.

● Yes. You can do a full end-to-end test against the real GitHub without
  anything reaching ponder.org.uk.

  Already done, against the mock GitHub: I ran the four extension scenarios that
  npm run test:extension doesn't include, and all pass:
  - changeset: 14/14
  - drop: 19/19
  - list: 19/19
  - widget: 16/16

  So all seven scenarios pass. I can add these four to test:extension if you'd
  like, which would make it take a few minutes longer.

  What only a real browser and the real GitHub can test:
  - the real toolbar popup;
  - the permission prompt when you press Edit this page;
  - the icon at its real size;
  - an actual commit;
  - the Action rebuilding the site and the extension noticing the edit is
    published.

  Why this is safe: GitHub Pages serves ponder.org.uk from docs/ on main. The
  extension commits to ponder-infusion, the branch named in
  infusion/linkage.json. The Build site workflow runs on pushes to
  ponder-infusion and commits the rebuilt docs/ back to that same branch.
  Nothing public changes until you merge into main.

  How to run it (all yours to run):
  1. Push your current ponder work to ponder-infusion. The extension reads and
     writes the sources on that branch on GitHub. If they don't match the pages
     you're viewing, the editor still works but warns that the repository's
     source differs.
  2. Use a separate clone of ponder for the site you'll edit, e.g. in /tmp,
     checked out on ponder-infusion. The extension's commits and the Action's
     rebuilds land on the remote branch, so a working copy holding uncommitted
     changes, like your current one, would conflict when pulling them.
  3. In that clone: npm ci, then npm run build, then serve docs/ locally, e.g.
     npx http-server docs -p 8080. It needs a moduleOverrides file naming your
     Infusion checkout if the published Infusion 6 isn't current enough.
  4. Open http://localhost:8080/ in your browser with the extension reloaded.
     Click its button and press Edit this page. Allow access to localhost, make
     a small edit to a post and press Commit.
  5. Check on GitHub that the commit landed on ponder-infusion and that Build
     site runs.
  6. Run git pull in the clone after the build finishes, so the local server
     serves the new docs/. Reload the page; the extension should show your edit
     as published. It decides that from docs/fluid-trace.json, which the build
     updates.
  7. Revert the test edit afterwards on ponder-infusion, e.g. by a second edit
     through the extension.

  Two things this won't cover:
  - The page being served from a real https site rather than localhost. The
    extension asks for access per site, but the rest of the flow is the same.
  - Whether Pages publishes the rebuilt site. That only happens on a merge to
    main, and the publish-detection logic is the same either way.

  I haven't pushed anything or touched either repository's git state.

● Finding the transferred app. An organisation's OAuth Apps are listed under
  Developer settings at the bottom of its settings sidebar, not under
  Third-party access. The direct address is:

  https://github.com/organizations/fluid-project/settings/applications

  Some reasons it might not show there:
  - Only organisation owners see that page. A member, or someone with a narrower
    role, doesn't get the Developer settings section at all, even for an app
    they transferred in.
  - Your own Developer settings won't show it any more. It belongs to the
    organisation now.
  - Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps lists it only because you've
    signed in with it, and only lets you revoke access. It doesn't lead to the
    app's settings.

  If you're an owner and it still isn't there, the app's settings page has the
  address
  https://github.com/organizations/fluid-project/settings/applications/<number>,
  where <number> is the app's numeric id. Your browser history from before the
  transfer may have the old address with that number.

  Why it commits to ponder-infusion. It's the site's own setting, not the
  extension's. Each site names its repository and branch in its linkage
  configuration, and the extension commits wherever the page's linkage record
  says. For ponder that's infusion/linkage.json:

  "repo": "amb26/ponder",
  "branch": "ponder-infusion",

  It's temporary in that sense. ponder-infusion is where the Infusion-built
  version of ponder lives while main still holds the published site. The branch
  is tied together in two places:
  - branch in infusion/linkage.json, which tells the extension where to commit;
  - the trigger of .github/workflows/build-site.yml (on: push: branches: 
    [ponder-infusion]), which rebuilds the site after each edit.

  When the Infusion version replaces the current site on main, both change to
  main. From then on, edits made through the extension publish to ponder.org.uk,
  because Pages serves docs/ on main.

       1  # ponder.org.uk
       2 -Hugo build for ponder.org.uk                                   
       2 +                                                               
       3 +The sources of [ponder.org.uk](https://ponder.org.uk), a static
         + site built with **wend**. wend renders a site as one          
       4 +tree of [Infusion 6](https://github.com/fluid-project/infusion-
         +6) components, and publishes each page as plain HTML.          
       5 +Each page also carries a record of what it was built from, so t
         +hat the "Edit in Infusion" browser extension can edit          
       6 +the page in place and commit the edit back to this repository. 
       7 +                                                               
       8 +## Layout                                                      
       9 +                                                               
      10 +```                                                            
      11 +content/          The site's pages, in markdown with front matt
         +er - posts, docs, terms, standalone pages                      
      12 +static/           The site's own static files - images, papers,
         + stylesheets - copied as they are into the site                
      13 +wend.json         The site's configuration: its title, menus, a
         +uthor and the theme's parameters                               
      14 +wend.site.json    How wend builds this site: its modules, host 
         +document, editing configuration and static directories         
      15 +wend/             The site's own parts - see wend/README.md    
      16 +  site.html         The host document, which declares Infusion 
         +and imports every SFC of the site's modules                    
      17 +  editing.json      The editing configuration - the repository 
         +and branch edits are committed to, and what may be edited      
      18 +  sfc/shortcodes/   The site's shortcodes, as components       
      19 +packages/                                                      
      20 +  wend/             The build, and the parts any wend site shar
         +es - see packages/wend/README.md                               
      21 +  beautiful-wend/   The theme - see packages/beautiful-wend/REA
         +DME.md                                                         
      22 +docs/             The built site, which GitHub Pages publishes 
         +- written by the build, never edited by hand                   
      23 +notes/            Design notes and requirements gathered while 
         +building wend, to be moved elsewhere                           
      24 +checklinks.js     Checks that every link of the built site reso
         +lves - npm test                                                
      25 +```                                                            
      26 +                                                               
      27 +`packages/wend` and `packages/beautiful-wend` are kept in this 
         +repository until they are published to npm.                    
      28 +                                                               
      29 +## Building                                                    
      30 +                                                               
      31 +```                                                            
      32 +npm install                                                    
      33 +npm run build                                                  
      34 +```                                                            
      35 +                                                               
      36 +This writes the site to `docs/`, in a few seconds. Only pages w
         +hose markup has changed are rewritten, and pages               
      37 +which no longer exist are removed. Then serve `docs/` with any 
         +static server, e.g. `npx http-server docs`.                    
      38 +                                                               
      39 +The build uses Infusion 6 as installed in `node_modules`. To bu
         +ild against a checkout of Infusion instead, name it in a       
      40 +`moduleOverrides.json5` at the root, which is never committed: 
      41 +                                                               
      42 +```json5                                                       
      43 +[{"moduleName": "infusion-6", "baseDir": "../infusion-6/"}]    
      44 +```                                                            
      45 +                                                               
      46 +or pass `--infusion <dir>`. The other options of `node packages
         +/wend/js/buildSite.js` are:                                    
      47 +- `-o <dir>` writes the site elsewhere than `docs/`;           
      48 +- `--live true` keeps in each page the records from which it co
         +uld be made live again;                                        
      49 +- `--from M --limit N` renders just N pages from the Mth, e.g. 
         +while working on the theme.                                    
      50 +                                                               
      51 +## Writing content                                             
      52 +                                                               
      53 +A page is a markdown file under `content/`, whose URL follows i
         +ts path, e.g. `content/post/2025-03-20-ui-as-code.md` is       
      54 +`/post/2025-03-20-ui-as-code/`. Front matter, in YAML between `
         +---` lines or TOML between `+++` lines, gives its              
      55 +`title`, `date`, `tags`, `subtitle` and so on.                 
      56 +                                                               
      57 +Within the markdown:                                           
      58 +- **A shortcode**, e.g. `{{< figure src="..." caption="..." >}}
         +`, renders a component of the site's own                       
      59 +  `wend/sfc/shortcodes/`. Those which run in the browser, e.g. 
         +`{{< vizreactive >}}`, boot Infusion on their page             
      60 +  alone - see `bootLayers` in `wend/README.md`.                
      61 +- **A code fence** whose info string is a language followed by 
         +`live`, e.g. ` ```js live `, renders as a live example         
      62 +  of Infusion: an editor whose code is run, beside any view it 
         +defines. One followed by `syntax` is shown highlighted         
      63 +  and read-only.                                               
      64 +                                                               
      65 +## Publishing                                                  
      66 +                                                               
      67 +`.github/workflows/build-site.yml` builds the site whenever its
         + sources change on the branch named in                         
      68 +`wend/editing.json`, and commits the rebuilt `docs/` to that br
         +anch. GitHub Pages serves ponder.org.uk from `docs/` on        
      69 +`main`.                                                        
      70 +                                                               
      71 +## Editing in place                                            
      72 +                                                               
      73 +The "Edit in Infusion" extension for Chrome, from Infusion 6's 
         +`extension/edit-in-infusion/`, edits a page of the             
      74 +published site in place: its content, and the parts of its fram
         +ing which `wend/editing.json` lists, e.g. the footer.          
      75 +Each edit is committed, as the user signed in to GitHub, to the
         + repository and branch which `wend/editing.json` names.        
      76 +The workflow then rebuilds the site, and the extension recognis
         +es the edit as published once the rebuilt site's               
      77 +`docs/fluid-trace.json` records it.                            
      78 +                                                               
      79 +An edit to a file of the theme is not made in `packages/beautif
         +ul-wend` but in the site's own copy of the file, under         
      80 +`wend/override/`, which takes the place of the theme's - see `o
         +verrides` in `wend.site.json`.
