● I've finished the tidy-up. The configuration file is now wend/editing.json
  rather than branch-coordinates.json, because the file does more than name a
  branch. A rebuild of the site is identical to the one before apart from the
  expected path and hash changes, and all seven extension scenarios still pass.
  Nothing is committed.

  What I removed:
  - The Hugo leftovers: themes/, layouts/, archetypes/ and .hugo_build.lock.
    Nothing in the build read them; the theme lives on as
    packages/beautiful-wend.
  - snippets/, which held one pasted HTML snippet that's now replaced by the {{<
    vizreactive >}} component.
  - docs-infusion/, the output of an earlier build.
  - The unused smol-toml dependency, which was there for Hugo's TOML config.
    wend only reads YAML front matter.

  What I moved and renamed:
  - infusion/ is now wend/, holding the host page, the shortcodes and
    editing.json.
  - linkage.json is now editing.json. It names the repo and branch, but also
    which layers run in the browser and which parts of the page framing can be
    edited, so I didn't call it branch-coordinates.json. In wend.site.json its
    key is now editing, and the build code follows suit.
  - REQUIREMENTS.md, REQUIREMENTS-2.md and the old README (now hugo-port.md,
    marked as a historical record) are in a new top-level notes/, with a short
    index.

  What I rewrote:
  - A new top-level README.md: the layout, building, writing content (front
    matter, shortcodes, live examples), publishing, and editing in place.
  - wend/README.md: each part of wend/, with every field of editing.json
    explained.
  - The beautiful-wend README gained the component tree and the table of how
    Hugo template constructs map onto Infusion layers.
  - Comments: I removed every REQUIREMENTS.md Rn pointer, every pointer to
    Infusion's scratch reports, and every comment naming a deleted file, and
    rephrased where needed. I kept comments naming the upstream Beautiful Hugo
    template each component corresponds to, since that theme still exists and
    they help.
  - Config:
    - .gitignore now ignores moduleOverrides.json5, which says not to commit it
      but wasn't ignored.
    - The workflow now watches wend/** rather than infusion/** and themes/**.
    - package.json has a new description.

  Two things that would have broken the workflow's build on main:
  - The lockfile was out of date. infusion-6 had been added to package.json but
    never to package-lock.json, so npm ci would have failed. It's now in sync.
  - Infusion 6.3.0 is too old. It lacks fluid-liveExample.vue, which
    wend/site.html imports. I moved the site to 6.4.0, now on npm; wend's own
    package.json now requires 6.4.0 or later.

  Infusion side: the extension's test harness now finds the editing file through
  wend.site.json. The framing scenario expects the site's copy of the footer
  under wend/override/.

  Checks:
  - Rebuild: I built the site before and after into scratch folders, not docs/.
    With content hashes masked, every page is identical except the embedded
    record of what it was built from. There, the paths for edited framing files
    moved from infusion/override/ to wend/override/, and the SFC hashes changed
    because their comments changed.
  - Extension tests: all seven extension scenarios pass against the new layout:
    sign-in 27, framing 25, block editor 32, changeset 14, drop 19, list 19,
    widget 16.
  - Lint: I didn't add any lint errors. Ponder's lint config can't parse .vue
    files at all. The style errors in stabilization-regimes.js and one missing
    JSDoc in markdown.js were already there.
  - docs/ hasn't been rebuilt. Run npm run build before committing.

  Decision for you: the published site still won't build on GitHub. Even on
  6.4.0, the build fails against the npm copy of Infusion. The {{< vizreactive 
  >}} shortcode loads two files from Infusion's tests/ folder, and Infusion's
  .npmignore leaves tests/ out of the package. The options are:
  1. Ship those two files in the npm package.
  2. Have the workflow check out Infusion from git instead of npm.
  3. Move the visualiser's gallery and annotations from tests/ into src/. This
     is the cleanest, but it's a change to Infusion.

  Left alone, but you may want to change:
  - The page record keeps the "linkage" name (application/fluid-linkage+json).
    Renaming it touches the extension and the page format.
  - wend hard-codes ponder's names. Shortcodes become ponder.shortcode.<name>,
    and the code namespaces are ponder.trace and ponderMarkdown. wend can't be
    used for another site until that's generalised.
  - static/testjs/ is published but nothing links to it.
  - packages/wend/notes/github-sign-in.md stays where you asked for it, rather
    than in notes/.

● All three changes are done, and so is deleting static/testjs. The site builds
  and all seven extension scenarios pass: sign-in 27, framing 25, block editor
  32, changeset 14, drop 19, list 19, widget 16. Infusion's lint is clean.
  Nothing is committed.

  Visualiser files moved into src/. visual-signals-test-gallery.js and
  FluidSignalsTests-annotations.js are now in src/framework/vizReactive/, so
  they ship in the npm package. I updated the references in
  FluidSignalsVisualGraphTests.html, visual-signal-test.html and ponder's
  vizreactive shortcode. The ponder build to a scratch folder publishes both
  files, so the build failure against npm Infusion should be gone once a version
  with them is published. I didn't run FluidSignalsVisualGraphTests.html
  itself, because it loads d3 from a CDN.

  "Linkage" is now "provenance". The record in each page is a <script 
  id="fluid-provenance" type="application/fluid-provenance+json">. In wend's
  trace.js the functions are provenanceRecord, insertProvenance and
  provenanceType, and the hash input "build linkage" became "build provenance".
  The extension now reads edit.provenance, and the fluid-linkage-found message
  is fluid-provenance-found. I left alone everything that refers to the IL's
  $linkage: the theme's feature holders, fluid.editRoot and trace.linkingLayers.
  Pages published with the old record won't be recognised by the new extension,
  so the site and the extension need to go out together.

  ponder names are now wend in wend's code:
  - ponder.trace, ponder.siteModel, ponder.feeds and ponder.shortcode.* are now
    wend.*.
  - ponderMarkdown, ponderPageBoot and ponderWidgets are now wendMarkdown,
    wendPageBoot and wendWidgets.
  - Hashed published scripts are now prefixed wend- instead of ponder-.
  - The shortcode files are renamed to wend/sfc/shortcodes/wend-shortcode-*.vue,
    with their imports in site.html and the docs updated to match.
  - The extension's references to these names, and its stale comment paths, now
    point at wend.

  Kept as ponder's own, though you may want to change them:
  - The site's module id ponderSite and the stabilization animation's global
    ponderStabilization.
  - Some ponder-* CSS classes in the theme, e.g. ponder-date and ponder-title.
    These may be styled by the site's stylesheet, so renaming them could change
    how pages look.
  - ponder-specific values hard-coded in the theme: the giscus repo
    amb26/ponder, the media icons' Twitter and email links, and /css/ponder.css.
    Making it a general theme would mean turning these into site parameters.

  docs/ still needs rebuilding with npm run build before you commit.

  - trace.js:485 is the comment introducing it: "imported by every page, under

    modules, and adds its imports as %wendWidgets/<file>.

  It's the module name for widgets pasted into the site's widget directory,
  which every page then imports. Nothing in the extension uses the name.

  You probably won't find it in the built pages: the build only writes the
  module when the site actually has widgets, and ponder has none right now. You
  won't find it in docs/ either, because that hasn't been rebuilt since the
  rename. Under the old name, the widget scenario's pasted widget is what used
  to produce it.

● I found nothing that does the whole of what wend and the extension do
  together, but there is strong prior art for each part. The closest relative
  overall is Wikipedia's VisualEditor and Parsoid, not any static-site tool. I
  only read search summaries, not the projects' code, and the Parsoid and
  Webstrates points come from my own knowledge because the searches didn't turn
  them up.

  The combination I found nowhere else is:
  - The same component tree is booted over the published static page, in the
    browser.
  - The page itself names the sources, build scripts and Infusion copy it was
    built from, in its provenance record.
  - Edits are previewed by the build's own markdown pipeline, not a separate
    preview renderer.
  - Commits go straight to GitHub from the browser, with no server of your own.
  - The edit is confirmed as published when the rebuilt site's trace records it.

  1. Wikipedia's VisualEditor and Parsoid: the strongest precedent.
  - It edits the rendered page in place, on the live site.
  - It serialises the edit back to wikitext, the textual source.
  - To do that, Parsoid records the source offsets of each element in the HTML
    (data-parsoid, data-mw), which is the same idea as the provenance record.
  - The difference is that it depends on a server that converts in both
    directions. It isn't a static site, and the build pipeline doesn't run in
    the browser.

  2. Commercial visual editors for static sites: provenance in data attributes.
  - CloudCannon works on plain static HTML output. Attributes such as
    data-editable, data-path and data-key tie an element to a source file.
  - Sanity marks elements with data-sanity attributes or invisible encoded text,
    and an overlay reads them to offer click-to-edit.
  - Netlify's Visual Editor (formerly Stackbit) reportedly puts data-cms-edit-*
    attributes into the HTML at build time, mapping elements back to Markdown,
    JSON or YAML in git. That claim comes from a third-party guide.

  These are the same pattern as wend's provenance record. However, they edit
  inside the vendor's hosted editor or a running dev server, not the published
  page. In general the preview isn't produced by the site's own build code
  running in the browser.

  3. Git-backed contextual editing: TinaCMS.
  - It renders the editing preview with the site's own React components, and
    edits become git commits. It's the nearest to the isomorphic part.
  - It needs the site to be a React or Next.js app, with Tina's own bundle and
    backend in the loop, rather than booting over the plain published HTML.

  4. Small open-source in-place editors. These are the closest in spirit, but
  they edit HTML rather than a source that gets rendered.
  - Handpress edits a hand-written static site in place, and each save is a git
    commit. It keeps the source as a second DOM beside the page and targets
    edits by key, which is a lightweight form of provenance.
  - Blip is a browser visual editor that syncs to GitHub, aimed at flat-file
    HTML sites.
  - git-edit edits HTML elements marked with a class and data attributes, with
    live preview, and commits to GitHub through a proxy.
  - edit-mode does inline text editing on static HTML, but downloads the new
    file rather than committing.
  - GitMark is a Chrome extension for editing Markdown, but only on GitHub's own
    file view, not on the published site.

  5. Research on editing output back to source: Sketch-n-Sketch. This is the
  theory behind the question.
  - Sketch-n-Sketch runs a program that produces HTML or SVG. When you edit the
    output directly, it works out a change to the program that reproduces your
    edit, using trace links from output back to source.
  - FuseDM (2024) tries to remove the need for users to know about those links.
  - Both deal with general programs and don't touch publishing.
  - Webstrates has a different aim: the live DOM itself is the shared, persisted
    document, with no source and no static build. It sits at the opposite end
    of the design space.

  Where this leaves wend:
  - The provenance-in-the-page pattern is well established, in Parsoid,
    CloudCannon and Sanity.
  - Editing in place on the published page with commits to git exists, but only
    for HTML-as-source tools such as Handpress and Blip.
  - Previewing with the site's own components exists only inside app frameworks,
    such as TinaCMS.
  - I found no system that boots the build's own component tree and pipeline
    over a plain static page from published provenance, or that checks
    publication against a build trace.
  - If you write this up, the comparisons worth making are with Parsoid and
    VisualEditor (rendering back to source), CloudCannon (data-attribute
    provenance on static output) and Sketch-n-Sketch (the bidirectional theory).

  Sources:

  - git-edit (https://github.com/krispo/git-edit)
  - Blip (https://blipcms.com/)
  - edit-mode (https://github.com/christoph-det/edit-mode)
  - GitMark (https://github.com/ThinkMo/gitmark)
  - Markdown++ (https://github.com/emir/markdown-plus-plus)
  - gitzen (https://gitzen.dev/)
  - GitLab Static Site Editor (https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/v13.1
    .2-ee/doc/user/project/static_site_editor)
  - CloudCannon editable regions (https://community.cloudcannon.com/t/adding-edi
    table-regions-to-static-sites/476)
  - Sanity overlays
    (https://www.sanity.io/docs/visual-editing/visual-editing-overlays)

    (https://www.sanity.io/docs/visual-editing/visual-editing-without-react)

    et-up-visual-editing-on-a-headless-cms-frontend)
